iterations.theme: Što je EU Inc: europska regulativa, tržište kapitala i (ne)zrelost hrvatskog pravnog okvira

sections.subtitle: Iz volonterskog entuzijazma u 'sobe u kojima se odlučuje': kako je nastao CroStartup
sections.screenshot_description: Marijana Šarolić Robić na početku razgovora predstavlja udrugu CroStartup i zahvaljuje na pozivu
sections.content:
Nakon duže stanke, Domovina TV vraća se novom epizodom u kojoj voditelj za sugovornicu ima **Marijanu Šarolić Robić**, a tema je nova europska inicijativa poznata pod nazivom **EU Inc** – ideja o jedinstvenom, univerzalnom obliku trgovačkog društva na razini Europske unije.

Marijana Šarolić Robić na uvodno pitanje o tome tko je ona odgovara kroz priču o udruzi **CroStartup**, hrvatskoj udruzi koja, kako kaže, "gradi hrvatski start-up ekosustav" i postoji nešto više od četiri pune godine. Ističe da je riječ o grupi entuzijasta i volontera koji su vjerovali da znanje i iskustvo koje imaju dolaze u pravom trenutku da pokrenu stvari u Hrvatskoj i da se "stave u sobe u kojima se razgovara o stvarima važnima za sve start-upove", pa tako i hrvatske, na europskoj razini.

Inicijativa za osnivanje došla je od **Davora Runje**, tadašnjeg predsjednika CISEX-a, koji je, prepričava gošća, jednostavno rekao "ajde vi to napravite". Iako je prva reakcija bila skeptična – "opet još jedna udruga" – na kraju je prevagnulo pitanje "tko će kad neće nitko".

U upravni odbor pozvani su ljudi iz različitih dijelova ekosustava, među kojima gošća nabraja:

- **Srđana Kovačevića** iz Orke
- **Darka Jovišića** iz Robotike
- **Maju Brkljačić** iz Algebre
- **Marija Frančeševića** za CISEX
- **Božidara Pavlovića**, koji pokriva VC i business angel priču

Cilj je bio, kaže, potpuno volonterski gurnuti temu tehnološkog poduzetništva bliže mainstreamu i utvrditi što Hrvatskoj zapravo treba. Udruga je i dio **European Startup Networka**, jedne od dviju krovnih organizacija koje okupljaju start-up inicijative, uz **Allied for Startups**.
sections.subtitle_en: From Volunteer Enthusiasm to the 'Rooms Where Decisions Are Made': How CroStartup Was Born
sections.screenshot_description_en: At the beginning of the conversation, Marijana Šarolić Robić introduces the CroStartup association and expresses gratitude for the invitation
sections.content_en:
After a longer break, Domovina TV returns with a new episode in which the host's interlocutor is **Marijana Šarolić Robić**, and the topic is a new European initiative known as **EU Inc** – the idea of a single, universal form of company at the European Union level.

To the introductory question about who she is, Marijana Šarolić Robić answers through the story of the **CroStartup** association, a Croatian association that, as she says, "is building the Croatian start-up ecosystem" and has existed for slightly more than four full years. She points out that this is a group of enthusiasts and volunteers who believed that the knowledge and experience they have come at the right moment to get things moving in Croatia and to "put themselves into the rooms where things important for all start-ups are discussed", including Croatian ones, at the European level.

The initiative for its founding came from **Davor Runje**, then president of CISEX, who, the guest recounts, simply said "go ahead and do it". Although the first reaction was skeptical – "yet another association again" – in the end the question "who will if nobody will" prevailed.

People from different parts of the ecosystem were invited to the board of directors, among whom the guest lists:

- **Srđan Kovačević** from Orka
- **Darko Jovišić** from Robotika
- **Maja Brkljačić** from Algebra
- **Mario Frančešević** for CISEX
- **Božidar Pavlović**, who covers the VC and business angel story

The goal was, she says, completely voluntarily to push the topic of technological entrepreneurship closer to the mainstream and determine what Croatia actually needs. The association is also part of the **European Startup Network**, one of two umbrella organizations that bring together start-up initiatives, alongside **Allied for Startups**.

sections.subtitle: Kako je EU Inc uopće nastao: europski osnivači, Draghijev izvještaj i nepostojeće jedinstveno tržište
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava Draghijev izvještaj o konkurentnosti Europe i podatak o zanemarivoj trgovini među članicama
sections.content:
Na pitanje vodi li CroStartup EU Inc u Hrvatskoj, Marijana Šarolić Robić precizira: udruga tu temu **promovira**, ali sama inicijativa nastala je drugdje. Pokrenuli su je, objašnjava, europski osnivači koji su već napravili exite – spominje imena **Saimera Šefera** i **Lucijana Bruna**, Nizozemce i Belgijance koji su, budući da su na zrelim tržištima i u sjedištu događanja, prepoznali gdje je stvarna barijera.

Ta barijera, kaže, možda i nije toliko sam trenutak osnivanja tvrtke, koliko činjenica da pitanja poput **ESOP-a** (radničkog dioničarstva) i **prekograničnog investiranja u različite jurisdikcije** nisu riješena na razini EU. Ta je skupina, ističe, s inicijativom krenula pune dvije godine prije nego što ju je Europska komisija uopće prihvatila.

Paralelno se dogodila ono što gošća naziva "serendipity – sretna slučajnost koja nije slučajnost": **Mario Draghi** izdao je izvješće o konkurentnosti Europe u kojem je kao jedan od ključnih problema istaknuto da **jedinstveno europsko tržište zapravo ne postoji**. Trgovina među zemljama članicama, navodi, zanemariva je – spominje brojku od otprilike sedam do jedanaest posto, uz ogradu da se ne drži za točan podatak – a istodobno je riječ o tržištu od **450 milijuna kupaca** na koje svi ciljaju.

Na tom tragu nova Europska komisija, koju ponovno predvodi **Ursula von der Leyen**, po prvi je put imenovala **povjerenicu za start-upove**, Bugarku koja je na tu poziciju došla nakon **Marije Gabriel**, također Bugarke, koja je u ranijem mandatu otvarala iste teme. Komisija je potom pozvala europske start-upove da kažu što ih muči.
sections.subtitle_en: How EU Inc Came About in the First Place: European Founders, the Draghi Report, and the Non-Existent Single Market
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the Draghi report on European competitiveness and the data on negligible trade among member states
sections.content_en:
To the question of whether CroStartup leads EU Inc in Croatia, Marijana Šarolić Robić clarifies: the association **promotes** the topic, but the initiative itself originated elsewhere. It was launched, she explains, by European founders who have already made exits – she mentions the names of **Saimer Šefer** and **Lucijan Bruno**, Dutchmen and Belgians who, being in mature markets and at the headquarters of events, recognized where the real barrier is.

That barrier, she says, is perhaps not so much the moment of founding the company itself, as much as the fact that issues such as **ESOP** (employee share ownership) and **cross-border investment into different jurisdictions** are not resolved at the EU level. That group, she points out, set off with the initiative full two years before the European Commission accepted it at all.

In parallel, what the guest calls "serendipity – a happy coincidence that is not a coincidence" happened: **Mario Draghi** issued a report on the competitiveness of Europe in which it was highlighted as one of the key problems that **the single European market actually does not exist**. Trade among member states, she states, is negligible – she mentions a figure of roughly seven to eleven percent, with the caveat not to hold her to the exact figure – while at the same time it is a market of **450 million customers** that everyone is targeting.

Along these lines, the new European Commission, once again led by **Ursula von der Leyen**, appointed for the first time a **Commissioner for Startups**, a Bulgarian woman who came to that position after **Marija Gabriel**, also Bulgarian, who in her earlier mandate had opened up the same topics. The Commission then invited European start-ups to say what troubles them.

sections.subtitle: Hakaton 2025.: tri problema zbog kojih europski start-upovi bježe u Delaware
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća nabraja tri glavna problema europskih start-upova identificirana na hakatonu
sections.content:
U ožujku 2025. održan je hakaton na kojem su, prepričava Marijana Šarolić Robić, otvorene sve teme koje muče start-upove, i to razvrstane po fazama razvoja – od pre-seed i seed faze, preko scale-upa, do growth i exit faze. Cilj je bio identificirati što je najvažnije riješiti prvo, a moment se, kaže, savršeno poklopio s već pokrenutom EU Inc inicijativom.

Kristalizirala su se tri problema:

- **Nekorištenje benefita jedinstvenog europskog tržišta** – potencijal zajedničkog tržišta ostaje neiskorišten.
- **Prekogranične investicije** – ako ste hrvatski start-up, a dođe investitor iz Njemačke, on ne razumije hrvatsku dokumentaciju i ne želi uložiti ako ne osnujete GmbH. Isto vrijedi i obrnuto, kad hrvatski fond ulaže u njemačke start-upove, ili u bilo kojoj drugoj kombinaciji.
- **ESOP, odnosno radničko dioničarstvo** – start-upovi žele privući i zadržati najbolje ljude, ali ih u fazi razvoja ideje ili traženja product-market fita ne mogu platiti, pa im dodjeljuju equity. To pitanje, kaže gošća, nije bilo ispravno adresirano; neke zemlje poput **Irske** pokušale su, ali na kraju svi hrvatski – a vjeruje i europski – start-upovi moraju osnovati **UK LLC** ili otići u **Delaware** i napraviti *Incorporated*, oblik koji omogućava dodjelu dionica radnicima, suosnivačima ili ključnom osoblju.

Komisija je, ističe, tu temu uzela kao svoj *flagship* projekt, a dokaz je i to što gotovo dvije pune godine na razvoju regulative radi zajedno s Allied for Startups i European Startup Networkom.
sections.subtitle_en: Hackathon 2025: Three Problems Due to Which European Start-ups Flee to Delaware
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest lists the three main problems of European start-ups identified at the hackathon
sections.content_en:
In March 2025, a hackathon was held where, Marijana Šarolić Robić recounts, all the topics troubling start-ups were opened, sorted by development phases – from the pre-seed and seed phase, through scale-up, to the growth and exit phase. The goal was to identify what is most important to resolve first, and the timing, she says, coincided perfectly with the already launched EU Inc initiative.

Three problems crystallized:

- **Non-utilization of the benefits of the single European market** – the potential of the common market remains unutilized.
- **Cross-border investments** – if you are a Croatian start-up, and an investor comes from Germany, he does not understand Croatian documentation and does not want to invest unless you establish a GmbH. The same applies vice versa, when a Croatian fund invests in German start-ups, or in any other combination.
- **ESOP, that is, employee share ownership** – start-ups want to attract and retain the best people, but in the phase of developing the idea or searching for product-market fit they cannot pay them, so they grant them equity. That question, the guest says, had not been properly addressed; some countries like **Ireland** tried, but in the end all Croatian – and she believes European – start-ups have to form a **UK LLC** or go to **Delaware** and create an *Incorporated*, a form that enables granting shares to employees, co-founders, or key personnel.

The Commission, she points out, took that topic as its *flagship* project, and proof is also that for almost two full years it has been working on the development of the regulation together with Allied for Startups and the European Startup Network.

sections.subtitle: Zašto regulativa, a ne direktiva – i zašto je rok kraj ove godine
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava pravnu razliku između europske direktive i regulative
sections.content:
Gošća, koja je po struci pravnica i odvjetnica, posebno naglašava pravno-tehnički detalj koji je ključan za uspjeh EU Inc-a: riječ je o **regulativi**, a ne o direktivi.

Kod **direktive**, objašnjava, nakon objave u službenom glasniku EU svaka država članica ima pravo tekst "translatirati", odnosno hrvatski ili bilo koji drugi parlament u manjoj ili većoj mjeri inkorporira ga u postojeće zakone. Tu nastaje problem interpretacije – kako će se to prenijeti "doma".

Kod **regulative** (*regulation*) toga nema. Tekst je donesen jedinstveno i u tom se jedinstvenom obliku mora implementirati u svim državama članicama, na cijelom teritoriju EU. Tako je bilo s **GDPR-om**, tako je i s **AI Aktom** – dio je to novog legislativnog okvira koji pokušava unificirati zakone kako bi poduzetnici, građani i potrošači znali da imaju ista prava u svakoj članici, bez situacije u kojoj "Belgijanci kažu jedno, Hrvati drugo, a Nijemci treće".

Što se tiče zakonodavnog puta, Marijana Šarolić Robić opisuje trenutačni status: Europska komisija izradila je regulativu i predala je Europskom parlamentu, tekst je u javnom savjetovanju, a sada slijedi treća faza u kojoj **Europsko vijeće**, odnosno sve države članice, daju svoj amandman. Ideja je da se u **devetom mjesecu** održi finalni sastanak na kojem bi se usvojio konačni tekst, nakon čega bi on išao u Europski parlament i bio izglasan **do kraja ove godine**. To je, kaže, obećanje Komisije i nada se da će tako i biti.
sections.subtitle_en: Why a Regulation and Not a Directive – and Why the Deadline Is the End of This Year
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the legal difference between a European directive and a regulation
sections.content_en:
The guest, who is a lawyer and attorney by profession, particularly emphasizes the legal-technical detail that is crucial for the success of EU Inc: it is a **regulation**, and not a directive.

With a **directive**, she explains, after publication in the official journal of the EU, every member state has the right to "translate" the text, that is, the Croatian or any other parliament incorporates it to a lesser or greater extent into existing laws. That is where the problem of interpretation arises – how it will be transferred "at home".

With a **regulation** (*regulation*), there is none of that. The text is adopted uniformly and in that uniform form it must be implemented in all member states, across the entire territory of the EU. So it was with **GDPR**, so it is with the **AI Act** – it is part of a new legislative framework that attempts to unify laws so that entrepreneurs, citizens, and consumers know they have the same rights in every member state, without a situation where "the Belgians say one thing, the Croats another, and the Germans a third".

As for the legislative path, Marijana Šarolić Robić describes the current status: the European Commission drafted the regulation and submitted it to the European Parliament, the text is in public consultation, and now follows the third phase in which the **European Council**, that is, all member states, submit their amendment. The idea is to hold a final meeting in the **ninth month** where the final text would be adopted, after which it would go to the European Parliament and be voted on **by the end of this year**. That is, she says, the Commission's promise, and she hopes it will be so.

sections.subtitle: Što EU Inc konkretno donosi: isti papiri, osnivanje u 48 sati i 'Choose Europe First'
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća nabraja konkretne benefite EU Inc-a za osnivače i investitore
sections.content:
Konkretni ishod, objašnjava gošća, bio bi **jedinstveni dokument i jedinstveni zakon koji vrijedi u cijeloj EU**. Hrvatski start-upper osnovao bi kompaniju u Hrvatskoj, ali s istim setom dokumenata kao njemački ili francuski start-up.

Prednosti koje pritom nabraja:

- investitor koji dolazi **zna u što ulaže**, a *due diligence* postaje jednostavan
- postoji **jednostavan način dodjele dionica, odnosno udjela** ključnim ljudima, suosnivačima ili radnicima
- **osnivanje unutar 48 sati**

Naglašava i granice inicijative: teme poput **radnog i poreznog zakonodavstva** ostaju riješene nacionalnim zakonodavstvima, to nije ni ingerencija ni intencija EU. No EU Inc je, kaže, početak priče o tome da zaista imamo **"Choose Europe First"**, tehnološku suverenost i iskorištavanje potencijala jedinstvenog tržišta.

Njezina se nada svodi na dvoje: da se regulativa donese u formi koja omogućava implementaciju i da je države članice zaista tako i provedu – kako start-uperi ne bi zbog tih razloga **prerano** odlazili u UK i SAD. "Kad ste došli do faze unicorna pa vam fali kapitala, morate ići u Silicijsku dolinu", kaže, "ali sve ovo prije, a to su puno godina, možete ostati u Europi, odnosno u Hrvatskoj."
sections.subtitle_en: What EU Inc Concretely Brings: Identical Papers, Incorporation in 48 Hours, and 'Choose Europe First'
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest lists the concrete benefits of EU Inc for founders and investors
sections.content_en:
The concrete outcome, the guest explains, would be a **single document and a single law that applies across the entire EU**. A Croatian start-up founder would establish a company in Croatia, but with the same set of documents as a German or French start-up.

The advantages she lists in doing so:

- the incoming investor **knows what he is investing in**, and *due diligence* becomes simple
- there is a **simple way of granting shares, that is, stakes** to key people, co-founders, or workers
- **incorporation within 48 hours**

She also emphasizes the boundaries of the initiative: topics like **labor and tax legislation** remain resolved by national legislations, that is neither the remit nor the intention of the EU. But EU Inc is, she says, the beginning of the story of truly having **"Choose Europe First"**, technological sovereignty, and utilizing the potential of the single market.

Her hope boils down to two things: that the regulation be adopted in a form that enables implementation and that the member states really carry it out in that way – so that start-up founders do not leave for the UK and USA **prematurely** for those reasons. "When you reach the unicorn stage so you lack capital, you have to go to Silicon Valley," she says, "but all this before, and that is many years, you can stay in Europe, that is, in Croatia."

sections.subtitle: Hrvatski sudski registar bolji od njemačkog – i rupa koju je ostavio socijalizam
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća hvali hrvatski sudski registar i sustav e-Građani u usporedbi s Njemačkom
sections.content:
Voditelj postavlja praktično pitanje: osoba osnuje d.o.o. u Hrvatskoj i nema jednostavnog načina, kao u Delawareu, da bilo tko s tržišta kapitala potpiše **SAFE ugovor** i tako ubaci kapital u postojeću firmu. Nudi li neka europska država to danas?

Odgovor je – ne, a razlog su različite razine zrelosti pojedinih tržišta u EU. No Marijana Šarolić Robić tu iznosi i pohvalu na račun Hrvatske. **Hrvatski sudski registar** ocjenjuje kao izvrstan, jedan od najboljih u EU, upravo zato što je kroz priču s **e-Građanima** dosta digitalizirana javna uprava. "Vi ne biste vjerovali koliko je naš registar bolji nego njemački ili talijanski", kaže.

Na sastanku u **Ministarstvu pravosuđa, uprave i digitalne transformacije** rečeno joj je, prepričava, da tehnički gledano sustav mogu **odmah upogoniti** jer imaju svu infrastrukturu. Njemačka to nema i njima će biti velik problem uložiti kako bi zadovoljili rok od 48 sati koji Hrvatska već tehnički može ispuniti.

S druge strane, priznaje, ono što u Njemačkoj postoji – razvijeno opće **pravo društava** – u Hrvatskoj ne postoji, jer njemačka ekonomija nije imala "četrdeset i pedeset godina rupu socijalizma gdje je svo privatno vlasništvo nestalo, bilo pobrisano". Ta zrelost tržišta znači da je investitor – bio anđeo investitor, institucionalni VC fond ili bilo koji treći oblik – u boljoj poziciji lakše ući u društvo, uložiti kapital i kasnije dobiti povrat.

sections.subtitle_en: The Croatian Court Register Better Than the German One – and the Gap Left by Socialism
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest praises the Croatian court register and the e-Citizens system in comparison with Germany
sections.content_en:
The host poses a practical question: a person founds a d.o.o. in Croatia and there is no simple way, as in Delaware, for anyone from the capital market to sign a **SAFE agreement** and thus inject capital into the existing company. Does any European country offer that today?

The answer is – no, and the reason is the different levels of maturity of individual markets in the EU. But Marijana Šarolić Robić here also expresses praise at Croatia's expense. She assesses the **Croatian court register** as excellent, one of the best in the EU, precisely because through the story with **e-Građani** the public administration has been significantly digitized. "You wouldn't believe how much better our register is than the German or Italian one," she says.

At a meeting in the **Ministry of Justice, Administration and Digital Transformation**, she recounts, she was told that technically speaking they can **put the system into operation immediately** because they have all the infrastructure. Germany does not have that, and for them it will be a big problem to invest in order to meet the 48-hour deadline that Croatia can already technically fulfill.

On the other hand, she admits, what exists in Germany – developed general **corporate law** – does not exist in Croatia, because the German economy did not have "a forty- and fifty-year gap of socialism where all private property disappeared, was wiped out". That market maturity means that an investor – whether an angel investor, an institutional VC fund, or any third form – is in a better position to more easily enter a company, invest capital, and later obtain a return.

sections.subtitle: SAFE i CLA: alati iz Silicijske doline i njihove mučne lokalne izvedenice
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava SAFE i CLA ugovore te zašto se moraju prilagođavati lokalnim jurisdikcijama
sections.content:
Ideja iza EU Inc-a, kaže gošća, upravo je **fleksibilizacija tržišta kapitala** i to da alati koji već postoje profunkcioniraju i u Europi. Nabraja dva ključna:

- **SAFE** – *Simple Agreement on Future Equity*
- **CLA** – *Convertible Loan Agreement*

Oba su, ističe, izmišljena u **Silicijskoj dolini**, a ne u New Yorku koji također ima tržište kapitala – dakle dolaze iz tehnoloških kompanija i postali su industrijski standard. A tehnološka kompanija, argumentira, standard traži tamo gdje su najbolji, "a najbolji su u Silicijskoj dolini, manje-više". Možda će uskoro biti negdje drugdje, ali tamo se svi žele mjeriti – nitko ne želi "spuštati lopticu".

Svi ostali bili su prisiljeni te alate uzimati i prilagođavati lokalnim jurisdikcijama, praviti **derivate i izvedenice** koje funkcioniraju u nekoj mjeri, ali ne u pravom obliku. Za usporedbu navodi **UK**, gdje je dovoljno obavijestiti *Companies House* da ste promijenili shareholdera. U Hrvatskoj svi zajedno moraju kod bilježnika sve potpisati.

No i tu Hrvatska prolazi bolje od Njemačke. Iz razgovora s VC društvima koja rade i tu i tamo, prenosi, doznala je da potpisivanje kod njemačkog javnog bilježnika traje po **pet-šest sati**, na termin se čeka **tri-četiri mjeseca**, a trošak bilježnika za investiciju od 300.000 eura – što je tek nekakav pre-seed – iznosi kao "srednji rabljeni auto". "Mi smo u Hrvatskoj super što se toga tiče", zaključuje, uz ogradu da to ne znači da je dobro, nego samo da može biti puno gore.
sections.subtitle_en: SAFE and CLA: Silicon Valley Tools and Their Painful Local Derivatives
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains SAFE and CLA contracts and why they have to be adapted to local jurisdictions
sections.content_en:
The idea behind EU Inc, says the guest, is precisely the **flexibilization of capital markets** and having the tools that already exist function in Europe as well. She lists two key ones:

- **SAFE** – *Simple Agreement on Future Equity*
- **CLA** – *Convertible Loan Agreement*

Both were, she points out, invented in **Silicon Valley**, not in New York which also has a capital market – meaning they come from tech companies and have become the industry standard. And a tech company, she argues, seeks the standard where the best are, "and the best are in Silicon Valley, more or less". Maybe soon they will be somewhere else, but that is where everyone wants to measure themselves – nobody wants to "lower the bar".

Everyone else was forced to take those tools and adapt them to local jurisdictions, make **derivatives and spin-offs** that function to some extent, but not in their true form. For comparison she cites the **UK**, where it is enough to notify *Companies House* that you changed a shareholder. In Croatia, everyone together must go to a notary and sign everything.

Yet even here Croatia fares better than Germany. From conversations with VC firms operating both here and there, she relays, she learned that signing before a German notary takes **five to six hours**, an appointment is waited on for **three to four months**, and the notary cost for an investment of 300,000 euros – which is merely a pre-seed of sorts – amounts to the cost of a "mid-range used car". "We in Croatia are great as far as that is concerned," she concludes, with the caveat that this does not mean it is good, but only that it can be much worse.

sections.subtitle: Ugovor od dvjesto stranica ili od dvije: 'život se dogodi Ž'
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća kao pravnica objašnjava koncept prave volje stranaka i granice svakog ugovora
sections.content:
Voditelj primjećuje da SAFE ima svega pet stranica, dok minimalno pristojan ugovor o convertible loanu u Hrvatskoj ima petnaest stranica teksta – jer se mora pokriti svaki mogući članak zakona i svaki *edge case*.

Marijana Šarolić Robić tu unosi bitnu korekciju: broj stranica nije poanta. "Može biti na dvije stranice, to je nebitno. Problem je u tome da nije fleksibilno."

Kao pravnica i odvjetnica objašnjava da pravnici ugovore pišu po svom najboljem znanju, iskustvu i standardu industrije, ali: "Ti napraviš A-B-C-D ugovor, a **život se dogodi Ž**." Ne postoji ugovor koji pokriva sve – niti mora postojati. Ono što mora postojati zove se **prava volja stranaka**: u preambuli ugovora definira se što se točno želi postići, pa se kod svake devijacije koja nije predviđena vraćate na početne postavke i pitanje zašto ste uopće ušli u taj posao.

Dok postoji prava i dobra volja stranaka, kaže, nije važno pokriva li ugovor baš sve. Problem nastaje kada se ugovori grade s namjerom da se nekoga prevari ili da se bude pametniji – tada se gubi balans ravnopravnosti, a ugovore sklapate upravo kao ravnopravni partneri.

Zaključak je jasan: ugovor od dvjesto stranica također će nešto propustiti definirati, "zato što je to život", a onaj od dvije stranice može biti jednako dobar. "Nema tu bulletproof rješenja. Niti Amerikanci imaju bulletproof rješenje, niti Europljani – tako da nećemo ni mi kroz EU Inc, niti oni kroz Delaware Inc."
sections.subtitle_en: A Two-Hundred-Page Contract or a Two-Page One: 'Life Happens Z'
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest as a lawyer explains the concept of the true will of the parties and the limits of any contract
sections.content_en:
The host observes that a SAFE has merely five pages, while a minimally decent convertible loan contract in Croatia has fifteen pages of text – because every possible article of the law and every *edge case* must be covered.

Marijana Šarolić Robić here introduces an essential correction: the number of pages is not the point. "It can be on two pages, that is irrelevant. The problem is that it is not flexible."

As a jurist and attorney, she explains that lawyers write contracts to the best of their knowledge, experience, and industry standard, but: "You make an A-B-C-D contract, and **life happens Z**." There is no contract that covers everything – nor must there be. What must exist is called the **true will of the parties**: in the preamble of the contract it is defined what is specifically meant to be achieved, so with every deviation that was not foreseen you return to the initial premises and the question of why you entered into that deal in the first place.

As long as the true and good will of the parties exists, she says, it is not important whether the contract covers absolutely everything. The problem arises when contracts are built with the intention of deceiving someone or being smarter – then the balance of equality is lost, and you enter contracts precisely as equal partners.

The conclusion is clear: a contract of two hundred pages will also fail to define something, "because that's life", and one of two pages can be just as good. "There is no bulletproof solution here. Neither do the Americans have a bulletproof solution, nor do the Europeans – so neither will we through EU Inc, nor them through Delaware Inc."

sections.subtitle: Investitor i osnivač: partnerstvo koje funkcionira dok se ne poremeti povjerenje
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća opisuje odnos investitora i osnivača te trenutak kada nastupi distorzija povjerenja
sections.content:
Iz teme ugovora gošća prelazi na anatomiju odnosa između investitora i osnivača. Postavlja model: ona kao privatni investitor ima višak kapitala, druga strana ima ideju ili već razvijen proizvod ili uslugu, i ona daje novac jer ono što vidi nosi veći **opportunity cost**, odnosno veći prinos od alternativnih ulaganja – "ili ste mi vi zabavni, a to su novci koje mogu izgubiti". Oba su, ističe, potpuno legitimna razloga.

Dok postoji dogovor da investitor **ne ulazi u sferu odlučivanja** o proizvodu i usluzi, ne radi mikromenadžment, nego je zadovoljan time da rastu prihodi firme i time vrijednost njegova udjela – sve funkcionira. Što god se dogodilo, pa makar i korona, obje strane sjest će za stol i potpisati koje god dokumente treba: investitor da spasi svoju investiciju, a osnivač svoj posao, proizvod i uslugu.

Problem, upozorava, nastaje kada nastupi **distorzija povjerenja** – kada se pojavi skrivena agenda, kada jedna strana zapravo ne želi da druga prosperira, možda je želi "ubiti" jer želi veći tržišni udio, ili joj jednostavno "ide na živce". "Tu nema pomoći, nema ugovora koji će vam pomoći, svi ćete završiti na sudu, razvlačit ćete se, sve će boljeti i tu nema prosperiteta."

Suprotno tome, ako su obje strane usmjerene na to da firma raste, prodaje i da udio vrijedi više te da svi na kraju imaju više novca – sve je u redu. To je, podsjeća, i sama definicija trgovačkog društva: gospodarska djelatnost radi stvaranja profita, "ne govorimo o nikakvom čarati".
sections.subtitle_en: Investor and Founder: A Partnership That Works Until Trust Is Disrupted
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest describes the relationship between investor and founder and the moment when trust distortion sets in
sections.content_en:
From the topic of contracts, the guest moves on to the anatomy of the relationship between investor and founder. She sets up a model: she as a private investor has surplus capital, the other party has an idea or already developed product or service, and she gives money because what she sees carries a higher **opportunity cost**, that is, a higher return than alternative investments – "or you are fun to me, and that is money I can lose". Both, she points out, are completely legitimate reasons.

As long as there is an agreement that the investor **does not enter the decision-making sphere** regarding the product and service, does not micromanage, but is satisfied with company revenues growing and thus the value of his stake – everything works. Whatever happens, even if it is corona, both parties will sit down at the table and sign whatever documents are needed: the investor to save his investment, and the founder his business, product, and service.

The problem, she warns, arises when a **distortion of trust** occurs – when a hidden agenda appears, when one party actually does not want the other to prosper, maybe wants to "kill" it because it wants a larger market share, or it simply "gets on their nerves". "There is no help there, there is no contract that will help you, you will all end up in court, you will drag each other out, everything will hurt and there is no prosperity there."

Contrary to that, if both parties are focused on having the company grow, sell, and having the stake be worth more, and everyone ending up with more money in the end – everything is fine. That, she reminds, is the very definition of a commercial company: economic activity for the sake of generating profit, "we are not talking about any charity".

sections.subtitle: Od Magne Carte do Bastille: zašto se demokracija i tržište moraju vježbati
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća govori o nasljeđu Domovinskog rata i tranzicije te povijesnim usporedbama s Engleskom i Francuskom
sections.content:
Voditelj pita je li danas izazov napisati ugovor koji ima analognu vrijednost SAFE-a od pet stranica, a pritom pokrije sve moguće članke svih hrvatskih zakona. Gošća potvrđuje da jest, ali sve vraća na **zrelost tržišta**.

Podsjeća da je Hrvatska mala zemlja – "statistička pogreška na razini ekonomije EU" – s nasljeđem **Domovinskog rata** i **tranzicije**, te da tek zadnjih nekoliko godina živi dovoljno dobro da se kao društvo može baviti tim temama. "Mi smo morali proći kroz te procese", kaže.

Slijedi povijesna usporedba: **Engleska** je krenula s velikom poveljom sloboda u 13. stoljeću, **Francuska** je imala Bastilju i danas je u svojoj petoj republici, još uvijek ruši establišment. Zaključak: "Demokracija se vježba, društvo se razvija." Hrvatska kao mala zemlja ima sreću što je dio EU jer je vanjske silnice tjeraju da se razvija brže nego što bi sama mogla. A ta malenost, dodaje, ujedno je i prednost jer omogućava da se uzme ono što je dobro i skroji po vlastitoj mjeri.

Voditelj potom uspoređuje Hrvatsku i Njemačku: Njemačka ima preko 1.200 bankarskih licenci, što znači izrazito decentralizirano i otporno tržište – ako propadne jedna banka, ostalih 1.199 nastavlja raditi, dok je u Hrvatskoj takva situacija puno opasnija. No ono što kao građanin hvali jest hrvatski sustav digitalne identifikacije, kakav Njemačka nema.

Gošća se slaže i objašnjava to kulturološkim i povijesnim nasljeđem: **Bavarska je jedna Njemačka, centralna Njemačka druga, stare pruske zemlje treća**. "Kad živite u Njemačkoj, kužite: Berlin, Köln, Dresden, München – to su druge zemlje. Bez obzira što svi nose istu zastavu i žive iste vrijednosti, opet na kraju nisu."
sections.subtitle_en: From the Magna Carta to the Bastille: Why Democracy and the Market Must Be Practiced
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks about the legacy of the Homeland War and transition and historical comparisons with England and France
sections.content_en:
The host asks whether it is a challenge today to write a contract that has the analogous value of a five-page SAFE, while covering all possible articles of all Croatian laws. The guest confirms that it is, but returns everything to the **maturity of the market**.

She reminds that Croatia is a small country – "a statistical error at the level of the EU economy" – with the legacy of the **Homeland War** and the **transition**, and that only for the last several years has it lived well enough that as a society it can deal with these topics. "We had to go through those processes," she says.

A historical comparison follows: **England** started with the great charter of liberties in the 13th century, **France** had the Bastille and today is in its fifth republic, still tearing down the establishment. The conclusion: "Democracy is practiced, society develops." Croatia as a small country is fortunate to be part of the EU because external forces compel it to develop faster than it could on its own. And that smallness, she adds, is at the same time an advantage because it enables taking what is good and tailoring it to one's own measure.

The host then compares Croatia and Germany: Germany has over 1,200 banking licenses, which means a highly decentralized and resilient market – if one bank fails, the other 1,199 continue working, whereas in Croatia such a situation is much more dangerous. But what as a citizen he praises is the Croatian system of digital identification, which Germany lacks.

The guest agrees and explains this through cultural and historical heritage: **Bavaria is one Germany, central Germany another, the old Prussian lands a third**. "When you live in Germany, you get it: Berlin, Cologne, Dresden, Munich – those are different countries. Regardless of the fact that everyone carries the same flag and lives the same values, again in the end they are not."

sections.subtitle: 'Živjeti europski, a zarađivati američki' – kakvu EU zapravo želimo
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća citira Davora Runju o europskom životu i američkoj zaradi
sections.content:
Cijela priča o EU Inc-u, smatra Marijana Šarolić Robić, prilika je da svi građani EU promisle što točno žele od te Unije – "jer mi ju kreiramo, mi smo ju kreirali". Podsjeća na početke: zajednicu za ugljen i čelik, osnovanu s ciljem da se ne ponovi svjetski rat i da se stvori ideja zajedništva, možda i naivna, koja onda transcendira u nešto drugo.

**Geopolitika**, kaže, sada ide u korist Europi – iako je ružna – jer je tjera da promišlja što zapravo želi i da se postavi u odnosu na **Ameriku, Indiju i Kinu**, a da pritom ne zatvara granice, nego ostane otvorena i gostoljubiva, ali čuva ono što Europljane čini Europljanima.

Tu citira **Davora Runju**, koji je na jednom panelu prije godinu ili dvije rekao da "mi želimo živjeti europski, a zarađivati američki" – i raditi na američki način. Kako to dvoje pomiriti? Mora se, tvrdi, naći treći put. Američka rješenja ne dolaze u obzir jer se ne želi njihovo nasljeđe: "Nama je drago da imamo normalna četiri tjedna godišnjeg, a ne deset radnih dana; da čovjek ima vrijednost u sustavu, da ga se ne može od jučer do danas otpustiti." Ali, dodaje odmah, s druge strane ga se ne smije mjesecima držati na plaći samo zato što ga se ne može otpustiti – treba naći **dobru mjeru fleksibilnosti** u skladu s tim kakvo društvo se želi.

EU Inc je, ponavlja, tek **prvi korak**: osigurati da male kompanije – solo biznisi s nekoliko osnivača, mikropoduzeća s manje od deset zaposlenih – mogu narasti, mogu ostati male, ali i mogu prosperirati. Da nikoga ne koči to što je iz EU pa da naraste i postane, kako se izražava, "jedan izmišljam, Anthropic ili koji god".

Konkretno bi to značilo: osnovani ste kao hrvatski d.o.o., ali u formi EU Inc-a, uredno poslujete na području svih **27 zemalja članica**, otvarate svih 27 tržišta i pri primanju investicije nema razlike dolazi li fond iz Bratislave, Beča ili Osla. Registracija za hrvatske poduzetnike i dalje ostaje u hrvatskom registru – **interfejs je isti**, lokalni registri ostaju, a "workaround" je u pozadini.
sections.subtitle_en: 'Living European, While Earning American' – What Kind of EU Do We Actually Want
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest quotes Davor Runje on living European and earning American
sections.content_en:
The whole story about EU Inc, Marijana Šarolić Robić believes, is an opportunity for all EU citizens to reflect on what exactly they want from that Union – "because we create it, we created it". She recalls the beginnings: the Coal and Steel Community, founded with the goal that a world war not be repeated and that an idea of unity be created, perhaps even a naive one, which then transcends into something else.

**Geopolitics**, she says, is now working in Europe's favor – although it is ugly – because it compels it to reflect on what it actually wants and to position itself in relation to **America, India, and China**, while not closing borders, but remaining open and hospitable, yet preserving what makes Europeans European.

Here she quotes **Davor Runje**, who on a panel a year or two ago said that "we want to live European, while earning American" – and working the American way. How to reconcile the two? A third way must be found, she argues. American solutions are out of the question because their legacy is not desired: "We are glad to have a normal four weeks of vacation, not ten working days; that a person has value in the system, that one cannot be dismissed overnight." But, she immediately adds, on the other hand one must not be kept on payroll for months just because one cannot be dismissed – **a good measure of flexibility** must be found in accordance with what kind of society is wanted.

EU Inc is, she repeats, merely **the first step**: ensuring that small companies – solo businesses with a few founders, micro-enterprises with fewer than ten employees – can grow, can stay small, but also can prosper. That no one is hindered by being from the EU in growing and becoming, as she puts it, "one I'm making up, Anthropic or whichever".

Concretely that would mean: you are founded as a Croatian d.o.o., but in the form of EU Inc, you operate orderly across the territory of all **27 member states**, you open all 27 markets, and upon receiving an investment there is no difference whether the fund comes from Bratislava, Vienna, or Oslo. Registration for Croatian entrepreneurs still remains in the Croatian register – **the interface is the same**, local registers remain, and the "workaround" is in the background.

sections.subtitle: Tko se opire: bilježnici, sindikati i prednost malih digitaliziranih država
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća govori o lobijima koji se opiru implementaciji i primjeru Estonije
sections.content:
Iako je Ministarstvo pravosuđa poručilo da Hrvatska tehnički može krenuti "sutra", problem su druge članice koje to nemaju postavljeno. Tu Marijana Šarolić Robić otvara temu **otpora**.

Prednost imaju male države koje su otišle dalje. Kao primjer navodi **Estoniju**, koja se, kako kaže, boji Rusije pa je otišla "cijela digitalna".

Velike zemlje, s druge strane, imaju puno više lobija koji se opiru:

- **notari**, koji ne žele ostati bez svojih naknada
- **sindikati**, koji – koliko god tvrdili da su za radnike – ne žele dati radnicima pravo da budu udjeličari jer ne žele miješati rad i kapital

To je, sugerira, dio razloga zašto će se oko rokova i konačnog teksta voditi ozbiljna politička bitka.
sections.subtitle_en: Who Is Resisting: Notaries, Trade Unions, and the Advantage of Small Digitalized States
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks about lobbies resisting implementation and the example of Estonia
sections.content_en:
Although the Ministry of Justice stated that Croatia can technically start "tomorrow", the problem is other member states that do not have that set up. Here Marijana Šarolić Robić opens the topic of **resistance**.

Small states that have gone further have an advantage. As an example she cites **Estonia**, which, as she says, fears Russia so it went "completely digital".

Large countries, on the other hand, have far more lobbies resisting:

- **notaries**, who do not want to be left without their fees
- **trade unions**, which – however much they claim to be for workers – do not want to give workers the right to be shareholders because they do not want to mix labor and capital

That is, she suggests, part of the reason why a serious political battle will be fought over deadlines and the final text.

sections.subtitle: Kako mali poduzetnik u Hrvatskoj skuplja kapital? 'Tako da pita frenda ili mamu'
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća duhovito odgovara kako mali d.o.o. ili OPG danas može prikupiti 20.000 eura
sections.content:
Voditelj postavlja vrlo konkretno pitanje: kako mali **OPG** ili **d.o.o.** u Hrvatskoj danas može jednostavno prikupiti 20.000 eura?

Odgovor stiže bez uvijanja: "Tako da pita frenda ili mamu. To je jednostavna točka – tu prestaje jednostavnost. Ako nemaš prijatelja i nemaš mamu, onda si u problemu, fakat si u problemu."

Uzrok je opet kulturno i povijesno nasljeđe. Hrvatska je, kaže, **mlada demokracija s jako mladim tržištem kapitala**. Prije socijalizma postojale su **zadruge** i **zaklade** – oblici koji su omogućavali da se ljudi udruže i ulože znanje, vještine i višak novca, bilo da bi vratili nešto društvu, oplemenili postojeći posao ili zaradili sa strane. Svi ti razlozi, naglašava, potpuno su legitimni.

Problem hrvatskog tržišta kapitala mjeri konkretnim primjerima:

- **zadnji veliki IPO** bio je onaj **HT-a**, dakle početkom dvijetisućitih
- **Span** je, ističe, jedini tehnološki d.o.o. koji je napravio pravu konverziju i listao se na **Zagrebačku burzu**
- propulzivnost zadnjih godina dolazi gotovo isključivo od **dionica Končara**, koje su zbog veće likvidnosti pomaknule cijelo tržište

Ali sve to, upozorava, rezervirano je samo za javno listirana **dionička društva**. Ako ste d.o.o., de facto nemate način tako prikupiti kapital – a kamoli ako ste OPG. OPG naziva "totalnom izmišljotinom", crossoverom između obrta, slobodne djelatnosti i nečeg trećeg: nitko ne zna što je to točno ni u što bi se ulagalo – u osobu, u nju kao nositelja ili u ugovor o zakupu na tuđoj zemlji, jer malo OPG-ova ima dovoljno vlastite zemlje, a većina je na državnim ugovorima i zakupima.

Ipak, vidi i pomake: spominje inicijative poput **Founderbeama** preko **Zagrebačke burze** i **HBOR-a** kojima je cilj podići tržište kapitala i stvoriti **sekundarno tržište** za trgovanje udjelima u d.o.o.-ima.
sections.subtitle_en: How Does a Small Entrepreneur in Croatia Raise Capital? 'By Asking a Friend or Mom'
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest wittily answers how a small d.o.o. or family farm (OPG) today can raise 20,000 euros
sections.content_en:
The host poses a very concrete question: how can a small **OPG** or **d.o.o.** in Croatia today simply raise 20,000 euros?

The answer arrives without beating around the bush: "By asking a friend or mom. That is the simple point – that's where simplicity ends. If you don't have friends and you don't have a mom, then you're in trouble, you're really in trouble."

The cause is again cultural and historical legacy. Croatia is, she says, a **young democracy with a very young capital market**. Before socialism, there were **cooperatives** and **foundations** – forms that enabled people to unite and invest knowledge, skills, and surplus money, whether to give something back to society, enhance an existing business, or earn on the side. All those reasons, she emphasizes, are completely legitimate.

She measures the problem of the Croatian capital market with concrete examples:

- the **last major IPO** was that of **HT**, that is, in the early 2000s
- **Span** is, she points out, the only tech d.o.o. that made a true conversion and listed on the **Zagreb Stock Exchange**
- the propulsiveness of recent years comes almost exclusively from **Končar shares**, which due to greater liquidity moved the entire market

But all of that, she warns, is reserved only for publicly listed **joint-stock companies**. If you are a d.o.o., de facto you have no way to raise capital like that – let alone if you are an OPG. She calls OPG a "total concoction", a crossover between a craft, freelance activity, and something third: nobody knows what it is exactly or what one would invest in – into the person, into them as the carrier, or into a lease agreement on someone else's land, because few OPGs have enough land of their own, and most are on state contracts and leases.

Nevertheless, she also sees shifts: she mentions initiatives like **Founderbeam** via the **Zagreb Stock Exchange** and **HBOR** whose goal is to lift the capital market and create a **secondary market** for trading stakes in d.o.o. companies.

sections.subtitle: Udjel u firmi jednako vrijedan kao apartman na moru – samo što to nitko ne doživljava tako
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća uspoređuje ulaganje u udjel u firmi s kupnjom apartmana na moru
sections.content:
Marijana Šarolić Robić vjeruje da će EU Inc pomoći stvaranju svijesti o tržištu kapitala, a paralelno spominje i vijest koju je pročitala u medijima – da Vlada namjerava poticati građane da ulažu i u nešto osim štednje i nekretnina, kroz vlastite investicijske portfelje.

No tu, kaže, ulazimo u pitanje **financijske pismenosti** – i one građanske i one poduzetničke, da uopće razumijete u što ulažete. Uz to je potrebno i **brzo tržište s mehanizmima likvidnosti**: kad nešto propada, da se brzo može zatvoriti, staviti u stečaj ili predstečaj, likvidirati – da se brzo ulazi i izlazi, a ne da agonija traje generacijama. Kao primjere takvih agonija navodi **staru štednju** i **Agrokor**.

A ključni problem, tvrdi, nije zakonska podloga nego **ljudska percepcija**: "Mi to sve doživljavamo dosta osobno. Ne razumijemo, kad imamo firmu, da ta firma nije naša – naši su udjeli. Firma je pravna osoba i tu nastane glavni problem."

Zato, objašnjava, nije moguće da vlasnik firme s jednim zaposlenim u pet-šest klikova proda jedan posto firme na tržištu – jer **tržišta nema**, jer nitko ne želi kupovati te male firme. Potrebna je društvena svijest da je legitimno ulagati u tuđu firmu: da netko kupi 50 posto firme jednako kao što bi kupio **apartman na moru** koji daje agenciji na rentanje i od kojeg očekuje prinos – bez petljanja u operativu, uz to da osnivač i dalje bude direktor i vraća dio dobiti, te uz mogućnost da se pri izlasku brzo nađe novi kupac za taj udjel.

"Ne možeš imati to tržište dok nemaš svijest ljudi koji uopće razumiju da je to imovina jednako kao i nekretnina, jednako kao i novci na računu", zaključuje, dodajući da pravni sustav uvijek dolazi kasnije – on je "samo kaputić koji se oblači na ljudske odnose".
sections.subtitle_en: A Stake in a Company Just as Valuable as an Apartment by the Sea – Only Nobody Perceives It That Way
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest compares investing in a stake in a company with buying an apartment by the sea
sections.content_en:
Marijana Šarolić Robić believes that EU Inc will help create awareness of the capital market, and in parallel mentions news she read in the media – that the Government intends to encourage citizens to invest in something other than savings and real estate, through their own investment portfolios.

Yet here, she says, we enter the question of **financial literacy** – both civic and entrepreneurial, to understand at all what you are investing in. In addition, a **fast market with liquidity mechanisms** is needed: when something fails, that it can be quickly closed, put into bankruptcy or pre-bankruptcy, liquidated – to enter and exit quickly, rather than agony lasting for generations. As examples of such agonies she cites **old foreign currency savings** and **Agrokor**.

And the key problem, she argues, is not the legal foundation but **human perception**: "We perceive all of that quite personally. We do not understand, when we have a company, that that company is not ours – our shares are ours. The company is a legal entity and that is where the main problem arises."

Therefore, she explains, it is not possible for the owner of a company with one employee to sell one percent of the company on the market in five or six clicks – because **there is no market**, because nobody wants to buy those small companies. A social awareness is needed that it is legitimate to invest in someone else's company: for someone to buy 50 percent of a company just as they would buy an **apartment by the sea** that they hand over to an agency for renting and from which they expect a return – without meddling in operations, with the founder remaining the director and returning part of the profit, and with the possibility that upon exit a new buyer is quickly found for that stake.

"You cannot have that market until you have the awareness of people who understand at all that this is an asset just like real estate, just like money in an account," she concludes, adding that the legal system always comes later – it is "only a little coat put on human relationships".

sections.subtitle: Obiteljske firme pred zidom: kad nasljednici ne žele, a kupca nema
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava problem prijenosa obiteljskih firmi i profesionalizacije uprave
sections.content:
Nedostatak tržišta udjelima ima, upozorava gošća, vrlo konkretnu i bolnu posljedicu – **problem obiteljskih firmi**.

Opisuje tipičan scenarij: djeca ne žele, ne mogu ili im se jednostavno ne da preuzeti firmu kao nova generacija. U tom trenutku vlasnik mora napraviti **profesionalizaciju uprave**, jer će inače cijeli biznis – koji može imati 25 ili 50 zaposlenih – nestati odlaskom osobe koja je bila "gazda", budući da ne postoji tržište koje bi to kupilo.

Idealan ishod, priznaje, jest da postoji konkurent koji vas želi kupiti pa preuzme sve ugovore o radu i sve dobavljače – "mrak" – ali to se, kaže, neće dogoditi u vrlo malom broju slučajeva.

Rješenje je opet u stvaranju tržišta na kojem je potpuno legitimno ulagati u udjele. Ne očekuje da će to raditi svi, ali smatra da je potrebna **kritična masa** ljudi koji imaju viška novca i znanja te su spremni kupiti udjel u firmi ne petljajući se u operativu, nego doživljavajući to isključivo kao investiciju.
sections.subtitle_en: Family Businesses Up Against the Wall: When Heirs Do Not Want It, and There Is No Buyer
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the problem of transferring family businesses and professionalizing management
sections.content_en:
The lack of a market in company shares has, the guest warns, a very concrete and painful consequence – the **problem of family businesses**.

She describes a typical scenario: the children do not want to, cannot, or simply do not feel like taking over the company as the new generation. At that moment the owner must carry out a **professionalization of management**, because otherwise the entire business – which may have 25 or 50 employees – will disappear with the departure of the person who was the "boss", since there is no market that would buy it.

The ideal outcome, she admits, is that there is a competitor who wants to buy you and takes over all employment contracts and all suppliers – "fantastic" – but that, she says, will happen in a very small number of cases.

The solution is again in creating a market where it is completely legitimate to invest in shares. She does not expect everyone to do that, but considers that a **critical mass** of people who have surplus money and knowledge and are ready to buy a stake in a company without meddling in operations, but viewing it exclusively as an investment, is needed.

sections.subtitle: Bilježnik u jedan dan, a ne šest mjeseci: koliko se toga stvarno promijenilo
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća opovrgava tvrdnju da se na upis kod bilježnika i suda čeka mjesecima
sections.content:
Voditelj iznosi tezu o odlasku javnom bilježniku, potpisivanju papira i čekanju šest mjeseci na upis udjela. Marijana Šarolić Robić se odlučno ne slaže: "Nije baš tako. To je bilo tako nekad prije."

Govori iz vlastitog iskustva – kaže da ima skoro 48 godina i da je 2002. počela raditi kao mali vježbenik, kada je situacija zaista tako izgledala. Danas je, tvrdi, potpuno druga priča, a glavni problem je to što **ljudi nemaju sve papire**, a ne sustav.

Izuzetak je zagrebački sud, gdje postoje *backlogovi* zbog posljednja dva štrajka i odlaska dobrih ljudi zbog plaća – ali to, naglašava, nije problem suda, nego **demografije Hrvatske**. Na bilo kojem sudu izvan Zagreba, kaže, upis dobijete za jedan do dva dana. Ako imate bilježnika koji je predmet unio kroz sustav – što je danas moguće – može biti gotovo u roku od jednog dana.

Objašnjava i zašto: bilježnici su usred digitalne transformacije dobili mogućnost, kao i kod zemljišnih knjiga, da sami upišu apsolutno sve i odgovaraju za točnost, dok sud de facto samo zaključa unose, pregleda, zaključa i javno objavi.

"Ta priča više nije ni blizu", kaže. Trošak je, u odnosu na Njemačku, zanemariv – ne tvrdi da je malen, ali je zanemariv.
sections.subtitle_en: A Notary in One Day, Not Six Months: How Much Has Truly Changed
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest refutes the claim that one waits for months for registration with a notary and the court
sections.content_en:
The host presents the thesis of going to a public notary, signing papers, and waiting six months for the registration of shares. Marijana Šarolić Robić resolutely disagrees: "It's not quite like that. That was how it was sometime before."

She speaks from her own experience – she says she is almost 48 years old and that in 2002 she started working as a young trainee, when the situation really looked like that. Today, she claims, it is a completely different story, and the main problem is that **people do not have all the papers**, not the system.

The exception is the Zagreb court, where *backlogs* exist due to the last two strikes and the departure of good people because of salaries – but that, she emphasizes, is not a problem of the court, but of **Croatia's demographics**. At any court outside Zagreb, she says, you get the registration in one to two days. If you have a notary who entered the case through the system – which is possible today – it can be done within a day.

She also explains why: notaries in the midst of digital transformation received the capability, as with land registries, to enter absolutely everything themselves and be responsible for accuracy, while the court de facto only closes entries, inspects, closes, and publishes publicly.

"That story is no longer even close," she says. The cost, compared to Germany, is negligible – she does not claim it is small, but it is negligible.

sections.subtitle: Zašto odvjetnik u Silicijskoj dolini naplaćuje tisuće dolara za petnaest minuta
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća govori o cijeni pravnih usluga i valorizaciji znanja u Hrvatskoj i SAD-u
sections.content:
Nastavljajući o troškovima, gošća naglašava da te stvari **ne mogu biti besplatne**. Prepričava kako joj se klijent žalio koliko mu je odvjetnik u Silicijskoj dolini naplatio za petnaest minuta savjetovanja – "nekoliko tisuća dolara". Njezin je odgovor bio jednostavan: zato što je tržište takvo. "Oni zarađuju toliko i žele platiti jer vide vrijednost. Kod nas tržište nije takvo i ne vide vrijednost u onome što mi donesemo kao profesionalci."

Sustav, upozorava, nije jednodimenzionalan – svi su dionici te priče: bilježnici, pravnici, odvjetnici i poduzetnici. "Mi svi kreiramo tu stvarnost, svi moramo lobirati, gurati da se pomaknemo u nešto što želimo postati. Ne možemo biti Amerika, mi nismo Amerika niti UK."

Ipak, njezina je ocjena da je u zadnjih dvadeset godina napravljen **strašan pomak**. Ono što frustrira jest to što se vidi koliko se još može, pa neostvareni potencijal stvara dojam da nije napravljeno ništa – a jest.

Kao ilustraciju nudi anegdotu s početka karijere: pisalo se na trgovačkom papiru, hrpa sudaca nije imala računala, ljudi su kompjutere kupovali vlastitim novcem, a suci su doslovno sami tipkali jer njihovi suradnici nisu znali pisati na računalima. "To govorimo o 2000-ima, ne o 1954. – govorimo o 2006., 2007., 2008. i 2009."

Pomak je, kaže, ogroman, pogotovo s pametnim telefonima i sustavom e-Građani, i u privatnoj i u profesionalnoj sferi – "puno bolje nego u nekim zemljama kojima se divimo". Ali to košta, i profesionalizacija ima svoj trošak: "Ne treba preplatiti, ali ako donosi vrijednost, treba biti plaćeno."
sections.subtitle_en: Why a Silicon Valley Lawyer Charges Thousands of Dollars for Fifteen Minutes
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks about the price of legal services and the valorization of knowledge in Croatia and the USA
sections.content_en:
Continuing on costs, the guest emphasizes that these things **cannot be free**. She recounts how a client complained to her about how much a lawyer in Silicon Valley charged him for fifteen minutes of consultation – "several thousand dollars". Her response was simple: because the market is like that. "They earn that much and want to pay because they see value. With us the market is not like that and they do not see value in what we bring as professionals."

The system, she warns, is not one-dimensional – all are stakeholders in that story: notaries, lawyers, attorneys, and entrepreneurs. "We all create that reality, we all have to lobby, push to move into something we want to become. We cannot be America, we are not America nor the UK."

Still, her assessment is that in the last twenty years a **tremendous leap** has been made. What frustrates is seeing how much more can be done, so unrealized potential creates the impression that nothing has been done – but it has.

As an illustration she offers an anecdote from the beginning of her career: writing was done on business paper, a bunch of judges did not have computers, people bought computers with their own money, and judges literally typed themselves because their associates did not know how to write on computers. "We are talking about the 2000s, not 1954 – we are talking about 2006, 2007, 2008, and 2009."

The progress is, she says, enormous, especially with smartphones and the e-Citizens system, both in the private and professional sphere – "much better than in some countries we admire". But that costs, and professionalization has its cost: "One shouldn't overpay, but if it brings value, it should be paid."

sections.subtitle: Firmu možete osnovati online – i tada počinju klasične početničke greške
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća nabraja tipične greške kod samostalnog osnivanja firme putem online sustava
sections.content:
Voditelj kao primjer dobre prakse navodi **start.gov.hr**, sustav koji svakome omogućuje da jednostavno osnuje firmu. Gošća potvrđuje – može i preko **FINA-e** ili na druge načine.

Problem nastaje, upozorava, čim je situacija imalo kompleksnija. Ljudi podcijene stvar, naprave sve sami i naprave "sve one glupe početničke greške". Sustav je, objašnjava paradoks, takav da ljudi zapravo ne žele jednostavnu firmu – žele kompleksnu firmu, ali plaćati kao da je jednostavna.

Nabraja tipične greške:

- **zarez u nazivu firme** koji zaborave izbrisati, pa se poslije ljute odakle taj zarez – a za promjenu se opet mora kod bilježnika
- **neobična podjela udjela** kad je osnivača više: aplikacija to ne podržava jer je nemoguće predvidjeti sve ljudske ideje
- **pogrešno upisane djelatnosti**, jer ljudi to ne shvaćaju ozbiljno pa misle da mogu napisati bilo što

Svoju poantu ilustrira usporedbom: "Kad ideš kod frizera, znaš koliko si platio i kod kojeg si frizera došao. Ako radiš stvari sam, popravljaš si zube i radiš frizuru, onda dobiješ i takav output." Zato i postoje profesionalci – da ošišaju, poprave zube, ili da odvjetnik i javni bilježnik pruže uslugu koja donosi vrijednost.

U krajnjoj liniji, dodaje, iza toga stoji **cijela profesija koja garantira da će posao biti napravljen kako treba**. "Ne mogu sve stvari biti toliko liberalne da ih sve radimo sami, jer onda cijele struke prestaju biti potrebne. To je isto u redu da se kao društvo dogovorimo, samo moramo biti svjesni što to nosi sa sobom – da onda ne možemo reći da je netko to napravio krivo i pozvati ga na odgovornost. Onda smo svi sami krivi."
sections.subtitle_en: You Can Form a Company Online – and That's When the Classic Beginner Mistakes Start
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest lists typical mistakes in forming a company on one's own via the online system
sections.content_en:
The host cites as an example of good practice **start.gov.hr**, a system that enables anyone to simply form a company. The guest confirms – it is also possible via **FINA** or in other ways.

The problem arises, she warns, as soon as the situation is at all more complex. People underestimate the matter, do everything themselves, and make "all those silly beginner mistakes". The system is, she explains the paradox, such that people actually do not want a simple company – they want a complex company, but to pay as if it were simple.

She lists typical mistakes:

- **a comma in the company name** that they forget to delete, and later get angry where that comma came from – and for a change one must go to a notary again
- **an unusual division of stakes** when there are multiple founders: the application does not support it because it is impossible to foresee all human ideas
- **improperly registered activities**, because people do not take it seriously and think they can write whatever

She illustrates her point with a comparison: "When you go to a hairdresser, you know how much you paid and which hairdresser you came to. If you do things yourself, fix your own teeth and do your own hair, then you get that kind of output too." That is why professionals exist – to cut hair, fix teeth, or for a lawyer and a public notary to provide a service that brings value.

Ultimately, she adds, behind that stands **an entire profession that guarantees the job will be done properly**. "Not all things can be so liberal that we do them all ourselves, because then entire professions cease to be necessary. It is also fine for us as a society to agree on that, only we must be aware of what that brings with it – that then we cannot say someone did it wrong and hold them accountable. Then we are all to blame ourselves."
