sections.subtitle: Zaglavljeni u devedesetima: zašto je za promjenu sjedišta firme još uvijek potreban temeljni akt
sections.screenshot_description: Marijana Šarolić Robić objašnjava da je Zakon o trgovačkim društvima ostao u devedesetima
sections.content:
Razgovor s tehničkih tema o digitalizaciji naglo skreće u politiku u trenutku kada voditelj postavlja naizgled banalno pitanje: zašto promjena sjedišta firme uopće mora biti komplicirana procedura. Odgovor Marijane Šarolić Robić je nedvosmislen – **to nije tehnički, nego politički problem**.

"To je problem toga što smo mi ostali u devedesetima po pitanju Zakona o trgovačkim društvima", kaže gošća, dodajući kako je riječ o pitanju političkog lobiranja. Zakonski okvir nastao je u vrijeme kada je, kako slikovito kaže, u Hrvatskoj bilo "tri i pol firme", a glavni cilj bio je spasiti postojeća poduzeća od jugoslavenskih načina rada i uspostaviti novi sustav. Taj je okvir tada bio potpuno legitiman, ali danas proizvodi apsurde poput obveze mijenjanja temeljnog akta zbog promjene sjedišta.

Ključna poanta je pitanje odgovornosti: nitko to neće promijeniti umjesto poduzetnika. **"Bilježnike i političare baš boli briga. Mi smo ti koji imamo bol i mi moramo drajvati promjenu"**, poručuje. Poduzetnici, prema njezinu mišljenju, moraju "stiskati" političare i – što je još važnije – **učiniti sebe relevantnima kao glasačku skupinu**, jer je to jedini mehanizam koji tjera zakonodavca da mijenja propise.

Gošća priznaje da u sustavu ima puno gluposti i da je frustracija opravdana, ali odbacuje pasivnost: način da se nešto promijeni nije govoriti "trebalo bi", nego da se netko toga primi i to promijeni. "Imaš snage koliko imaš, imaš koncentracije koliko imaš, pa ćeš pomalo stvari mijenjati."
sections.subtitle_en: Stuck in the Nineties: Why a Foundational Act Is Still Required to Change a Company's Registered Seat
sections.screenshot_description_en: Marijana Šarolić Robić explains that the Companies Act remained in the nineties
sections.content_en:
The conversation from technical topics on digitalization turns abruptly into politics at the moment when the host poses a seemingly banal question: why changing a company's seat must be a complicated procedure at all. Marijana Šarolić Robić's answer is unequivocal – **this is not a technical, but a political problem**.

"That is a problem of us having stayed in the nineties regarding the Companies Act," says the guest, adding that it is a question of political lobbying. The legal framework was created at a time when, as she vividly puts it, there were "three and a half companies" in Croatia, and the main goal was to save existing enterprises from Yugoslav ways of working and establish a new system. That framework was completely legitimate back then, but today it produces absurdities such as the obligation to change the foundational act due to changing the seat.

The key point is the question of responsibility: nobody will change this instead of the entrepreneurs. **"Notaries and politicians really couldn't care less. We are the ones who have the pain and we must drive the change"**, she messages. Entrepreneurs, in her opinion, must "press" politicians and – what is even more important – **make themselves relevant as a voting group**, because that is the only mechanism that forces the legislator to change regulations.

The guest admits that there is a lot of foolishness in the system and that frustration is justified, but rejects passivity: the way to change something is not to say "it should be", but for someone to take hold of it and change it. "You have as much strength as you have, you have as much focus as you have, so you will change things gradually."

sections.subtitle: Ulazak u sobu u kojoj se odlučuje: kako udruga gura teme u javni prostor
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava kako CroStartup pokušava ući u sobe u kojima se donose odluke
sections.content:
Upravo je taj mehanizam, objašnjava Šarolić Robić, razlog postojanja udruge CroStartup. Cilj je bio "osvijestiti i ući u sobu u kojoj se priča" te jasno artikulirati stav: **ovo misle hrvatski start-upovi, ovo nam je relevantno, a ovo ne želimo i iz tih razloga.**

No tu se otvara i ključna dilema svakog zagovaranja. "Uvijek je pitanje, kada vas je puno u sobi, jeste li dovoljno važni da se vaš argument čuje i uvaži – ili treba doći na vlast", kaže gošća. Time razgovor prirodno prelazi na temu političkog angažmana, koji ona ocjenjuje **potpuno legitimnim i "jako potrebnim"**.

Politički aktivizam za nju je oblik odgovornosti prema društvu, jednako dobrodošao kao i građanske inicijative. "Ne ide bez toga", zaključuje kratko.

Voditelj na to ističe asimetriju koja mnoge iritira: politika vodi državu iz vlastitih interesa, plaće se isplaćuju iz državnog proračuna i nadprosječne su, dok istovremeno volonteri iz civilnog sektora pokušavaju napraviti dobre stvari – besplatno. Gošća se ne buni protiv te dijagnoze, ali odbija je prihvatiti kao izgovor: **"To je društvo u kojem mi živimo i mi smo ti koji moramo reći – to mi je u redu, a to mi nije u redu i to moramo mijenjati."** Podsjeća da zato i postoji Bastilja u povijesti i demokratski izbori u sadašnjosti, te da svatko ima i aktivno i pasivno biračko pravo. Njezina poruka je sažeta u jednu rečenicu: "Ako ti se nešto ne sviđa – nisi drvo, pomakni se."
sections.subtitle_en: Entering the Room Where Decisions Are Made: How the Association Pushes Topics into Public Space
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains how CroStartup tries to enter the rooms where decisions are made
sections.content_en:
Precisely that mechanism, explains Šarolić Robić, is the reason for the existence of the CroStartup association. The goal was to "raise awareness and enter the room where discussions take place" and clearly articulate the position: **this is what Croatian start-ups think, this is relevant to us, and this we do not want and for these reasons.**

Yet here opens the key dilemma of any advocacy. "It is always a question, when there are many of you in the room, whether you are important enough for your argument to be heard and respected – or whether one needs to come to power," says the guest. With that, the conversation naturally transitions to the topic of political engagement, which she assesses as **completely legitimate and "greatly needed"**.

Political activism for her is a form of responsibility toward society, just as welcome as civic initiatives. "It cannot go without that," she concludes briefly.

The host points to the asymmetry that irritates many: politics runs the state out of self-interest, salaries are paid from the state budget and are above average, while at the same time volunteers from the civil sector try to do good things – for free. The guest does not object to that diagnosis, but refuses to accept it as an excuse: **"That is the society we live in and we are the ones who have to say – this is fine with me, and this is not fine with me and we have to change this."** She reminds that this is why the Bastille exists in history and democratic elections in the present, and that everyone has both active and passive voting rights. Her message is summarized in one sentence: "If you don't like something – you're not a tree, move."

sections.subtitle: Sedam tisuća preferencijalnih glasova bez mandata: anatomija izbornog nesrazmjera
sections.screenshot_description: Voditelj iznosi analizu preferencijalnih glasova i nesrazmjera u dodjeli mandata
sections.content:
Voditelj potom iznosi rezultate vlastite analize posljednjih izbora, u kojoj je složio rang-listu najvećih dobitnika i gubitnika, dostupnu, kako navodi, na stranici **izbori.domovina.ai**. Ono što mu je najsulUdnije jest činjenica da osoba koja je skupila gotovo **7.000 preferencijalnih glasova nema mjesto u Saboru**, dok ga ima osoba s tek nekoliko stotina, odnosno stotinjak i nešto glasova.

Preračunato, tvrdi voditelj, riječ je o tome da je pojedini zastupnik dobio **82 puta veću ovlast s obzirom na izlaznost, odnosno 132 puta veću ovlast mjereno brojem birača**.

Odgovor gošće je smiren, ali oštar prema političkom establišmentu. O tome se, kaže, govori već od drugih parlamentarnih izbora – od trenutka kada je riješeno pitanje Podunavlja i kada je Hrvatska napokon imala teritorijalni integritet – ali "ne govori se u dovoljno širokom krugu jer to nas većinu običnih građana nažalost zamara".

Zaključak je jednostavan i neugodan: **izborni sustav se nije mijenjao jer političkom establišmentu odgovara takav kakav jest.** Za promjenu je potrebna kvalificirana većina, a kad god su pojedine opcije bile u poziciji nešto mijenjati – nisu. "Očito taj sustav paše onako kako je nacrtan na početku", kaže Šarolić Robić, dodajući da problemi s reprezentativnošću nisu hrvatski specijalitet – i Sjedinjene Države imaju sličan problem sa svojim izbornim mehanizmom.
sections.subtitle_en: Seven Thousand Preferential Votes Without a Mandate: Anatomy of Electoral Disproportion
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host presents an analysis of preferential votes and disproportion in the allocation of mandates
sections.content_en:
The host then presents the results of his own analysis of the latest elections, in which he compiled a ranking list of the biggest winners and losers, available, as he states, on the website **izbori.domovina.ai**. What strikes him as most absurd is the fact that a person who gathered almost **7,000 preferential votes does not have a seat in the Sabor**, while a person with merely a few hundred, that is, a hundred and some votes, has one.

Recalculated, the host claims, it is a matter of an individual MP having received **82 times greater authority with respect to turnout, that is, 132 times greater authority measured by the number of voters**.

The guest's answer is calm, but sharp toward the political establishment. That, she says, has been discussed ever since the second parliamentary elections – from the moment when the Podunavlje issue was resolved and when Croatia finally had territorial integrity – but "it is not talked about in a wide enough circle because that, unfortunately, tires most of us ordinary citizens".

The conclusion is simple and unpleasant: **the electoral system has not changed because it suits the political establishment just as it is.** A qualified majority is needed for change, and whenever individual options were in a position to change something – they didn't. "Apparently that system fits the way it was drawn at the beginning," says Šarolić Robić, adding that problems with representativeness are not a Croatian specialty – the United States also has a similar problem with its electoral mechanism.

sections.subtitle: "Ljudi su ginuli da bismo mogli zaokružiti krug": izlazak na izbore kao moralna obveza
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća emotivno govori o izlasku na izbore kao građanskoj odgovornosti
sections.content:
Na pitanju izlaznosti gošća zauzima svoj najstrastveniji ton u cijelom razgovoru. Demokracija se, upozorava, **neće dogoditi sama od sebe**; na njoj treba raditi, bilo da je čovjek za to plaćen ili radi aktivistički, iz uvjerenja da društvo može bolje.

Prvi i najosnovniji korak je izlazak na izbore. "Moraju otići aktivno glasati, a ne dići ruke", kaže, ističući da bi bila **za uvođenje kazne za one koji ne izađu**. Argument koji nudi nije pravni, nego moralni i povijesni: *"Ljudi su ginuli zato da bismo mi mogli otići tamo i zaokružiti taj krug. Toliko je nemoralno ne otići, dići guzicu – da budem prosta – i na taj se dan pojaviti na izborima."*

Uz sam čin glasovanja, ide i domaća zadaća: uzeti si vremena, proučiti što kandidati govore, provjeriti je li to u skladu s vlastitim vrijednostima i što znači za budućnost djece i države. Onima koji to ne rade poručuje kratko – **"nemoj mi prigovarati"**.

Pravo birati i biti biran, naglašava, nije nešto što je Hrvatskoj dala Europska unija, nego je izborena vlastitim snagama i predstavlja izravnu posljedicu Domovinskog rata. Zato je, po njezinu sudu, apsolutno nedopustivo ne izaći na izbore – i to na **sve** izbore: lokalne, parlamentarne, predsjedničke i europske. Bez toga, zaključuje, nema ni promjene Zakona o trgovačkim društvima ni zakrpane rupe na cesti ispred kuće.
sections.subtitle_en: "People Died So That We Could Circle the Ballot": Turning Out to Vote as a Moral Obligation
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks emotionally about turning out to vote as a civic responsibility
sections.content_en:
On the question of voter turnout, the guest adopts her most passionate tone in the entire conversation. Democracy, she warns, **will not happen on its own**; it needs to be worked on, whether a person is paid for it or works activist-style, out of the conviction that society can do better.

The first and most basic step is turning out to vote. "They must go actively vote, not throw up their hands," she says, emphasizing that she would be **in favor of introducing a fine for those who do not turn out**. The argument she offers is not legal, but moral and historical: *"People died so that we could go there and circle that ballot. It is so immoral not to go, get off your ass – to put it bluntly – and show up for elections on that day."*

Along with the very act of voting comes homework: taking the time, studying what candidates are saying, verifying whether that aligns with one's own values and what it means for the future of children and the country. To those who do not do that, she messages briefly – **"don't complain to me"**.

The right to elect and be elected, she emphasizes, is not something the European Union gave to Croatia, but was won by its own forces and represents a direct consequence of the Homeland War. That is why, in her judgment, it is absolutely impermissible not to turn out to vote – and in **all** elections: local, parliamentary, presidential, and European. Without that, she concludes, there is neither a change to the Companies Act nor a patched pothole on the road in front of the house.

sections.subtitle: E-izbori: zašto dida u zadnjem selu u Lici određuje granice digitalne demokracije
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava demografske i sigurnosne prepreke elektroničkom glasovanju
sections.content:
Voditelj postavlja logično sljedeće pitanje: nije li apsurdno da građanin mora biti fizički prisutan na točno određenom mjestu u nedjelju od sedam do sedam? Gošća se slaže da je to nepraktično, ali nabraja niz razloga zbog kojih promjena nije trivijalna.

Prvi je **demografija i digitalna pismenost**. Velik dio stanovništva, kaže, nema pristup digitalnoj sferi jer se jednostavno ne zna snaći. Drugi je **sigurnost**: razina cyber-kriminala i, kako to naziva, "cijeli ovaj treći svjetski rat koji se vodi", ne dopušta jamstvo jednakog i sigurnog pristupa svima.

Zato zaključuje da je zasad **fizičko biračko mjesto najliberalnije rješenje** – jer se ne može osigurati da "u zadnjem selu u Lici taj dida koji nema ni struje ni vode" može glasati online. "A ovako smo svi jednaki", kaže.

Dodatni je problem trošak: e-izbori koštaju jako puno, a paralelno održavanje elektroničkih i fizičkih izbora značilo bi dvostruki budžet koji si, pita se, koja zemlja može priuštiti.

Paralelu vidi u sustavu e-Građana. Svi, kaže, "fingiramo" da su svi Hrvati otvorili elektroničke pretince, imaju elektroničke osobne iskaznice ili putovnice i mogu primati pismena od Porezne uprave i iz zemljišnih knjiga – **a svi znamo da nije tako**. Voditelj tu napominje da je broj korisnika ipak solidan te upućuje na podatke pučke pravobraniteljice.

Gošća upozorava na najopasniju posljedicu: postoje "cijele klase ljudi koji su ostali bez svojih građanskih prava" jer je sustav otišao naprijed brže od njih. Najbanalniji primjer koji navodi jest upis u zemljišne knjige koji promakne jer čovjek nije pogledao pismeno stavljeno u elektronički pretinac, a fikcija dostave je nastupila. Time, upozorava, **raste i mogućnost malverzacija**, jer cijela ta skupina građana nije adresirana.
sections.subtitle_en: E-Elections: Why Grandpa in the Last Village in Lika Determines the Boundaries of Digital Democracy
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains demographic and security obstacles to electronic voting
sections.content_en:
The host poses the logical next question: isn't it absurd that a citizen must be physically present at a specifically determined location on Sunday from seven to seven? The guest agrees that it is impractical, but lists a series of reasons why the change is not trivial.

The first is **demographics and digital literacy**. A large part of the population, she says, lacks access to the digital sphere because they simply do not know how to navigate it. The second is **security**: the level of cybercrime and, as she calls it, "this whole third world war that is being waged", does not allow for a guarantee of equal and secure access to everyone.

Therefore, she concludes that for now the **physical polling station is the most liberal solution** – because it cannot be ensured that "in the last village in Lika that grandpa who has neither electricity nor water" can vote online. "And this way we are all equal," she says.

An additional problem is cost: e-elections cost very much, and running electronic and physical elections in parallel would mean a double budget which, she wonders, what country can afford.

She sees a parallel in the e-Citizens system. Everyone, she says, is "faking" that all Croatians have opened electronic mailboxes, have electronic identity cards or passports, and can receive documents from the Tax Administration and land registries – **and we all know that is not the case**. The host here notes that the number of users is nonetheless solid and points to data from the Ombudsperson.

The guest warns of the most dangerous consequence: there are "entire classes of people who have been left without their civil rights" because the system moved forward faster than they did. The most banal example she gives is a land registry entry that is missed because a person did not look at the document placed in the electronic mailbox, and statutory service occurred. With that, she warns, **the possibility of malpractices also grows**, because that entire group of citizens is not addressed.

sections.subtitle: Dvostruki model glasovanja i zašto se izborno pravo ne dira olako
sections.screenshot_description: Voditelj iznosi prijedlog izbora između fizičkog i online glasovanja
sections.content:
Voditelj nudi konkretan prijedlog. Budući da već danas birač koji želi promijeniti biračko mjesto to mora prijaviti sedam dana ranije kroz sustav, logično bi bilo, tvrdi, ponuditi **dvije opcije: izlazak na biračko mjesto ili glasovanje online**, uz istu prijavu unaprijed. Time bi se, računa, smanjio broj biračkih mjesta, osigurao tranzicijski period za one koji nisu spremni, a možda i pedesetak posto građana glasalo bi s bilo koje lokacije.

U raspravi se pritom priznaje i osobna sklonost online glasovanju – "prva bih glasala samo online jer sam lijena" – ali uz jasan zaključak: **dok to nije moguće za sve, hodat će se na biračko mjesto.** Sustav mora biti jednostavan, siguran i razumljiv jednako onome tko ima 73 godine i onome tko ima 18, jednako onome tko živi na Visu i onome u Podravskoj Slatini.

Šarolić Robić upozorava da je pravo birati i biti biran jedno od **temeljnih prava svake uređene demokracije** te da nije slučajno što je hrvatski Ustav za promjenu izbornog sustava propisao najrigidniju većinu. Vjeruje da je Državno izborno povjerenstvo svjesno promjena koje se događaju i da o njima vodi računa.

Ključna je, kaže, razlika između onoga što je **operativno moguće** i onoga što je **građansko pravo** – a te dvije stvari treba pomiriti. Ono što se "nama na kavi čini lagano izvedivo" na terenu izgleda posve drukčije.

Zato predlaže metodologiju: uključiti se u politiku i procese mijenjanja propisa, napraviti prethodnu dijagnozu, izračunati koliko bi ljudi novim modelom bilo zakinuto, provesti **male pilote** i tek onda mijenjati. Razlog je ozbiljan: jednom izmijenjen izborni sustav teško se vraća na početne postavke. "To nije reverzibilan proces", naglašava, "i može se napraviti puno veća šteta nego što se čini da je jednokratna korist" – pogotovo kod biračkih prava.
sections.subtitle_en: The Dual Voting Model and Why Voting Rights Are Not Touched Lightly
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host presents a proposal for choosing between physical and online voting
sections.content_en:
The host offers a concrete proposal. Since already today a voter who wishes to change their polling station must register that seven days in advance through the system, it would be logical, he argues, to offer **two options: turning out at a polling station or voting online**, with the same advance registration. That way, he calculates, the number of polling stations would decrease, a transition period would be ensured for those who are not ready, and perhaps fifty percent of citizens would vote from any location.

In the discussion, personal inclination toward online voting is also acknowledged – "I would be the first to vote only online because I'm lazy" – but with a clear conclusion: **as long as that is not possible for everyone, people will walk to the polling station.** The system must be simple, secure, and understandable equally to someone who is 73 years old and someone who is 18, equally to someone who lives on Vis and someone in Podravska Slatina.

Šarolić Robić warns that the right to elect and be elected is one of the **fundamental rights of every orderly democracy** and that it is not by chance that the Croatian Constitution prescribed the most rigid majority for changing the electoral system. She believes that the State Electoral Commission is aware of the changes taking place and takes them into account.

The key, she says, is the difference between what is **operationally possible** and what is a **civil right** – and those two things need to be reconciled. What "seems to us over coffee easily feasible" looks entirely different on the ground.

Therefore she proposes a methodology: get involved in politics and the processes of changing regulations, make a preliminary diagnosis, calculate how many people would be disadvantaged by the new model, conduct **small pilots**, and only then make changes. The reason is serious: once modified, an electoral system is difficult to revert to initial settings. "That is not a reversible process," she emphasizes, "and far greater damage can be done than what seems to be a one-time benefit" – especially with voting rights.

sections.subtitle: "Hvala, ali ne hvala": zašto se gošća ne želi kandidirati
sections.screenshot_description: Marijana Šarolić Robić objašnjava zašto ne želi ući u politiku
sections.content:
Kada voditelj najavi da će se kandidirati na izborima 2028. i uputi joj poziv da mu se pridruži, odgovor stiže bez oklijevanja: **"Hvala, ali ne hvala."**

Obrazloženje je precizno. Politika je, kaže Šarolić Robić, jako težak i **javan posao** koji pretpostavlja da čovjek stvarno stavi opće dobro iznad osobnog te da postane javna osoba – pri čemu svi segmenti života postaju javni, uključujući djecu i prijatelje. "Nema više skrivanja", kaže, i dodaje da je to u redu i da tako mora biti, jer političar odlučuje o stvarima koje utječu na velike skupine ljudi: **"Ne postoji ideja privatnosti kod javnih osoba, kod političara tim više."**

Drugi razlog je sam proces ulaska u politiku – borba za svaki glas koja pretpostavlja veliku žrtvu, mnogo osobnih kompromisa i snažnu podršku neposredne okoline. Pitanje je, kaže, želi li netko svoje resurse potrošiti baš na to. Njezin odgovor je ne, ali bez omalovažavanja onih koji odluče drukčije – dapače, smatra to hvalevrijednim i želi im da uspiju provesti promjene zbog kojih su ušli u politiku.

Svoj izbor volontiranja kroz udruge objašnjava time što joj je civilni aspekt bliži, jednostavniji i neformalniji, ali i **slobodniji**: "Ne obvezuje me jer nisam na plaći kod nikoga i mogu potpuno otvoreno govoriti ono što mislim." Ne mora, kaže, kalkulirati što misli stranka i koliko se to slaže s njezinim osobnim vrijednostima.

Definicija politike koju nudi je klasična: **umijeće vođenja javnih afera i javnih tema**, gdje se stvari guraju skupljanjem bodova, bilo da je riječ o poziciji ili oporbi.
sections.subtitle_en: "Thanks, but No Thanks": Why the Guest Does Not Want to Run for Office
sections.screenshot_description_en: Marijana Šarolić Robić explains why she does not want to enter politics
sections.content_en:
When the host announces that he will run in the 2028 elections and extends an invitation for her to join him, the answer arrives without hesitation: **"Thanks, but no thanks."**

The explanation is precise. Politics is, says Šarolić Robić, a very difficult and **public job** that presupposes that a person really puts the common good above the personal and becomes a public figure – whereby all segments of life become public, including children and friends. "There is no more hiding," she says, and adds that that is fine and must be so, because a politician decides on things that affect large groups of people: **"There is no idea of privacy with public figures, with politicians even more so."**

The second reason is the very process of entering politics – fighting for every vote that presupposes great sacrifice, many personal compromises, and strong support from one's immediate environment. The question is, she says, whether someone wants to spend their resources specifically on that. Her answer is no, but without disparaging those who decide differently – on the contrary, she considers it praiseworthy and wishes for them to succeed in implementing the changes for which they entered politics.

She explains her choice of volunteering through associations by the fact that the civic aspect is closer, simpler, and more informal to her, but also **freer**: "It doesn't bind me because I am not on anyone's payroll and I can speak completely openly what I think." She does not, she says, have to calculate what the party thinks and how much that aligns with her personal values.

The definition of politics she offers is classic: the **art of managing public affairs and public topics**, where things are pushed by gathering points, whether on the side of the ruling majority or the opposition.

sections.subtitle: Zašto rečenica nezavisnog i rečenica stranačkog dužnosnika nemaju istu težinu
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava razliku između izjave nezavisnog i izjave stranačkog dužnosnika
sections.content:
Voditelj primjećuje da su i podcasti danas javna arena i da svatko može iznijeti stav. Gošća se slaže, ali uvodi bitnu distinkciju: **"Ovo što ja izreknem kao Marijana jest Marijanino mišljenje, a ono što bih izrekla kao članica bilo koje stranke ima potpuno drugu konotaciju."**

Razlog nije u kvaliteti argumenta, nego u **političkoj moći i resursima**. Onaj tko sjedi u stranci koja ima moć u određenoj političkoj areni nosi sa sobom mogućnost mijenjanja, odlučivanja i – ključno – **budžete koji prate te odluke**. Nezavisni glas može biti izgovoren u javnoj areni, ali "osim ako to netko tko ima budžet i resurse ne prigrli, to će ostati samo izgovoreno". Čovjek će se, kaže ironično, osjećati bolje jer je to rekao, ali problem ostaje implementacija.

Razgovor se potom dotiče decentralizacije. Voditelj ističe da je umjetna inteligencija "pojela" znanje i raznijela ga u svaki kutak svijeta te da će se sve centralizirano samo istopiti. Gošća to pozdravlja kao **"najbolje što se moglo dogoditi"**, ali dodaje ozbiljnu ogradu.

Decentralizirano znanje, upozorava, pretpostavlja da ljudi **uče** kako ga koristiti. "To je ono što me najviše strah kod AI-a – da jedan od deset ljudi želi učiti, a s AI-em moraš učiti. I onda imamo problem ovih devet koji neće htjeti učiti." Voditelj zaključuje da onda imamo i vlast kakvu tih deset zaslužuje, a gošća pomiče odgovornost na kolektiv: pitanje je koliko smo se mi ostali angažirali, a koliko onaj jedan koji je sjeo, eksperimentirao, skužio pravila igre i napravio svoj okvir.
sections.subtitle_en: Why a Sentence by an Independent and a Sentence by a Party Official Do Not Carry the Same Weight
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the difference between a statement by an independent and a statement by a party official
sections.content_en:
The host observes that podcasts today are also a public arena and that anyone can state a position. The guest agrees, but introduces an essential distinction: **"What I say as Marijana is Marijana's opinion, but what I would say as a member of any party has a completely different connotation."**

The reason is not in the quality of the argument, but in **political power and resources**. Whoever sits in a party that has power in a particular political arena carries with them the possibility of changing, deciding, and – crucially – **the budgets that follow those decisions**. An independent voice can be spoken in the public arena, but "unless someone who has the budget and resources embraces it, that will remain only spoken". A person will, she says ironically, feel better for having said it, but the problem remains implementation.

The conversation then touches upon decentralization. The host points out that artificial intelligence has "eaten" knowledge and dispersed it to every corner of the world and that everything centralized will simply melt away. The guest welcomes this as **"the best thing that could have happened"**, but adds a serious caveat.

Decentralized knowledge, she warns, presupposes that people **learn** how to use it. "That is what scares me most about AI – that one in ten people wants to learn, and with AI you must learn. And then we have the problem of these nine who will not want to learn." The host concludes that then we also have the governance that those ten deserve, and the guest shifts the responsibility to the collective: the question is how much the rest of us engaged, and how much that one person who sat down, experimented, figured out the rules of the game, and made their own framework.

sections.subtitle: Rupa na cesti kao politički program: zašto nezavisni pobjeđuju na lokalnoj razini
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava zašto građani na lokalnoj razini biraju nezavisne kandidate
sections.content:
Voditelj navodi podatak s portala nezavisnih kandidata: oko **270 gradova i općina** vode ljudi koji nisu članovi političkih stranaka. Gošća u to lako vjeruje, jer je lokalna politika, kaže, "jako osobna" i zapravo **apolitična** – nije važno je li netko iz HDZ-a, SDP-a, Možemo ili bilo koje druge opcije.

Važno je nešto sasvim drugo, nabraja:
- je li rupa na cesti zakrpana,
- radi li starački dom kako spada,
- imamo li dom zdravlja,
- što je sa školama i vrtićima,
- kako rade mali biznisi,
- koje je radno vrijeme kafića,
- gdje ribar može iskrcati ribu.

To je, kaže, **prava javna politika**. I upravo je to razlog zašto nezavisni prolaze: oni dođu, poslušaju te teme i o njima govore na lokalnom radiju, televiziji ili internetu – dakle o stvarima koje su ljudima bliske. Građanin ih bira jer mu je obećao konkretnu stvar i jer ga poznaje: "znam ju i kako će mi ona kad me vidi na cesti reći – pitat ću je svaki put za tu rupu".

Tu se, tvrdi, krije i **odgovornost političara da ispuni predizborno obećanje**. Na lokalnoj razini je to lako provjerljivo: rupa je ili zakrpana ili nije. Na državnoj razini odgovornost se razvodnjava – "krivi su ovi prije, kriva je Vlada, kriva je EU, krivo je more, uvijek je netko drugi kriv" – i stvara se privid da se ništa ne može, iako se, kaže, može jako puno.

Problem velikih stranaka vidi u tome što su otišle u "filozofske sfere" i izgubile **rapport** s biračima. Nitko, ističe, ne pita saborskog zastupnika što je učinio od onoga što je obećao na predizbornom skupu: "Mi njih ne pitamo, mi njima damo vlast i onda ih poslije ništa ne obvezuje, čak ni ono što su napisali." Predizborne programe, dodaje sarkastično, "ChatGPT bi valjda napisao bolje" – a *delivery on promise*, nažalost, nema.

Korijen problema vraća na birače: "Tu je opet problem nas koji ne vježbamo demokraciju." Kada većina ne izađe, odlučuju oni koje su stranke aktivirale i oni koji glasaju po defaultu, pa se ostatak glasova rasprši. **"Demokracija se neće pobrinuti sama za sebe. Mi pojedinci se moramo pobrinuti da se demokracija pobrine za sve nas."** Modalitet glasovanja – internetsko bankarstvo, e-Građani ili olovka na papiru – pritom je posve nevažan; problem je, kaže, u supstanci.
sections.subtitle_en: A pothole in the road as a political program: why independents win at the local level
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains why citizens choose independent candidates at the local level
sections.content_en:
The host cites data from the independent candidates' portal: about **270 cities and municipalities** are led by people who are not members of political parties. The guest easily believes this, because local politics is, she says, "very personal" and actually **apolitical** – it does not matter whether someone is from HDZ, SDP, Možemo, or any other option.

Something completely different is important, she lists:
- whether the pothole in the road is patched,
- whether the nursing home works properly,
- whether we have a health center,
- what about schools and kindergartens,
- how small businesses operate,
- what the cafe working hours are,
- where a fisherman can unload fish.

That is, she says, **real public policy**. And that is precisely the reason why independents succeed: they come, listen to these topics, and speak about them on local radio, television, or the internet – that is, about things that are close to people. A citizen chooses them because they promised him a concrete thing and because he knows them: "I know her, and how she will say to me when she sees me on the road – I will ask her every time about that hole".

There, she claims, also lies the **responsibility of politicians to fulfill a pre-election promise**. At the local level, it is easily verifiable: the hole is either patched or it is not. At the national level, responsibility is diluted – "those before are to blame, the Government is to blame, the EU is to blame, the sea is to blame, someone else is always to blame" – and the illusion is created that nothing can be done, although, she says, a great deal can be done.

She sees the problem of large parties in the fact that they have gone into "philosophical spheres" and lost **rapport** with voters. No one, she points out, asks a member of parliament what he did of what he promised at a campaign rally: "We do not ask them, we give them power and then afterwards nothing obligates them, not even what they wrote." Campaign programs, she adds sarcastically, "ChatGPT would probably write better" – and *delivery on promise*, unfortunately, is absent.

She returns the root of the problem to voters: "Here again is the problem of us who do not practice democracy." When the majority does not turn out, those activated by the parties and those who vote by default decide, so the rest of the votes are scattered. **"Democracy will not take care of itself. We individuals must make sure that democracy takes care of all of us."** The voting modality – internet banking, e-Građani, or pen on paper – is completely irrelevant in this regard; the problem, she says, is in the substance.

sections.subtitle: Pravo koje gotovo nitko ne koristi: svaki zastupnik dužan vas je primiti
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava da građani mogu tražiti termin kod saborskog i europskog zastupnika
sections.content:
Jedno od najkonkretnijih otkrića epizode gošća iznosi gotovo usput: **građani mogu doći kod bilo kojeg zastupnika u Hrvatskom saboru, dobiti termin i izložiti mu svoj problem** – i on ih mora saslušati. Isto vrijedi i za europske zastupnike. "Ako si član njegove stranke – tim više; a ako i nisi, ti si građanin RH i on je tvoj zastupnik, nebitno koja je stranka."

Voditelj priznaje da za tu mogućnost nije ni znao. Gošća pojašnjava da su saborska zgrada i takvi sastanci javni, da se mogu dovesti novinari, snimati – pa i zloupotrijebiti – ali suština ostaje: **građanin može tražiti da ga se primi, a zastupnik mu je dužan dati termin.** Ako odbije, kaže, "to jako dobro govori o njemu".

Usporedbu vuče s Engleskom i Sjedinjenim Državama, gdje zastupnik ide "od vrata do vrata" jer želi svaki glas i doslovno skuplja povratne informacije birača – od rupe na cesti do škole koja ne radi popodne i malog biznisa koji ne može dobiti dozvolu za rad subotom.

Važno je, upozorava, ne pogrešno shvatiti smisao tog prava. Zastupnik ne može i **ne smije** osobno intervenirati za pojedinca. Ali ako mu se javi umirovljenik koji je radio 42 godine i ne može ostvariti mirovinu, zastupnik može utvrditi da u Hrvatskoj postoji, primjerice, 37 tisuća ljudi u istoj situaciji, obratiti se Hrvatskom zavodu za mirovinsko osiguranje, pitati zašto se to događa i potom **predložiti izmjene i dopune zakona** ili tražiti od resornog ministarstva donošenje pravilnika. "Poanta je da slušaš svoje birače, vidiš koliko ih je u sličnoj poziciji i da temeljem obrazaca reagiraš u skladu sa svojim političkim programom."
sections.subtitle_en: A right almost no one uses: every representative is obliged to receive you
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains that citizens can request an appointment with a parliamentary and European representative
sections.content_en:
One of the most concrete revelations of the episode the guest presents almost in passing: **citizens can come to any representative in the Hrvatski sabor, get an appointment, and present their problem to him** – and he must listen to them. The same applies to European representatives. "If you are a member of his party – all the more reason; and even if you are not, you are a citizen of the Republic of Croatia and he is your representative, regardless of which party he is from."

The host admits that he did not even know about this possibility. The guest clarifies that the parliament building and such meetings are public, that journalists can be brought in, recorded – and even abused – but the essence remains: **a citizen can request to be received, and the representative is obliged to give him an appointment.** If he refuses, she says, "that speaks very well about him".

She draws a comparison with England and the United States, where a representative goes "door to door" because he wants every vote and literally collects feedback from voters – from a pothole in the road to a school that does not work in the afternoon and a small business that cannot get a permit to work on Saturdays.

It is important, she warns, not to misunderstand the purpose of this right. A representative cannot and **must not** intervene personally for an individual. But if a pensioner who worked for 42 years and cannot realize his pension reaches out to him, the representative can determine that in Croatia there are, for example, 37 thousand people in the same situation, contact the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute, ask why this is happening, and then **propose amendments to the law** or ask the relevant ministry to adopt an ordinance. "The point is that you listen to your voters, see how many of them are in a similar position, and that based on patterns you react in accordance with your political program."

sections.subtitle: Escape room o demokraciji: europski centar u Bakačevoj i zeleni tjedan zastupnika
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća opisuje europski centar u Bakačevoj i mogućnosti koje nudi građanima
sections.content:
Korijen problema, tvrdi Šarolić Robić, jest elementarna nepismenost o tome **kako demokracija uopće funkcionira**. Kao konkretan lijek navodi europski centar otvoren u petom mjesecu prošle godine u zagrebačkoj Bakačevoj ulici.

Ondje svaki građanin EU – uključujući Hrvate, strance i turiste – može ući i saznati imena svih europskih zastupnika, ne samo hrvatskih, o čemu govore i kada govore. Postoji čak i **escape room u kojem se posjetitelji mogu "igrati demokracije"** – Parlamenta, Europskog vijeća i Komisije – i naučiti kako politički proces izgleda. Sve je javno dostupno i besplatno, a slični centri postoje u većini zemalja EU s idejom da se ljudi uče o svojim građanskim pravima i da znaju "gdje su granice onoga što političari moraju", umjesto da je sve "zaokuljeno i zamumuljeno".

Kvaka je, naravno, u trudu: treba izaći van, odvojiti dva sata i proučiti to. "Nema tu plug and play", kaže. "Problem je što smo većina nas ljudi lijenčine i onda biramo najkraći mogući put."

Kada voditelj postavi hipotezu – može li 151 osoba ugovoriti sastanak sa po jednim zastupnikom kako bi se izborila za digitalnu promjenu sjedišta firme bez javnog bilježnika – gošća precizira terminologiju: **to više nije individualna predstavka, to je politički aktivizam i lobiranje.** I potpuno je legitimno; demokracija ga upravo omogućava.

Tu podsjeća i na jedan malo poznat mehanizam: europski parlamentarci imaju takozvani **zeleni tjedan**, kada su dužni vratiti se u matične zemlje i primati građane koji imaju primjedbe na bilo što u EU. To rade i hrvatski europarlamentarci, koji imaju svoje urede po Hrvatskoj i Zagrebu, gdje se mogu tražiti *office hours*. Na temelju prikupljenih povratnih informacija trebalo bi se nešto i dogoditi – no, kaže, "problem je što mi nemamo svijest da je to uopće moguće".
sections.subtitle_en: Escape room about democracy: the European center in Bakačeva and the green week of representatives
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest describes the European center in Bakačeva and the opportunities it offers to citizens
sections.content_en:
The root of the problem, claims Šarolić Robić, is elementary illiteracy about **how democracy even works**. As a concrete remedy, she cites the European center opened in the fifth month of last year in Zagreb's Bakačeva Street.

There, every EU citizen – including Croats, foreigners, and tourists – can enter and find out the names of all European representatives, not just Croatian ones, what they talk about and when they speak. There is even an **escape room in which visitors can "play democracy"** – of the Parliament, the European Council, and the Commission – and learn what the political process looks like. Everything is publicly available and free, and similar centers exist in most EU countries with the idea that people learn about their civil rights and know "where the boundaries of what politicians must do are", instead of everything being "wrapped up and mumbled up".

The catch, of course, is in the effort: one needs to go out, set aside two hours, and study it. "There is no plug and play here", she says. "The problem is that most of us people are lazy and then we choose the shortest possible path."

When the host poses a hypothesis – whether 151 people can schedule a meeting with one representative each in order to fight for the digital change of a company's registered office without a notary public – the guest clarifies the terminology: **that is no longer an individual petition, that is political activism and lobbying.** And it is completely legitimate; democracy precisely enables it.

Here she also recalls a little-known mechanism: European parliamentarians have a so-called **green week**, when they are obliged to return to their home countries and receive citizens who have remarks on anything in the EU. Croatian MEPs do this as well, who have their offices throughout Croatia and Zagreb, where *office hours* can be requested. On the basis of the collected feedback, something should happen – but, she says, "the problem is that we do not have awareness that this is even possible".

sections.subtitle: Tko bi trebao učiti građane demokraciji – i tko ih zapravo prima
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća govori o obrazovanju, kritičkom mišljenju i naslijeđu socijalizma
sections.content:
Na pitanje tko bi građane trebao naučiti kako sustav funkcionira, gošća je skeptična prema instituciji škole. "Tko bi to trebao učiti – vrtić, osnovna škola, srednja škola? Pa mi se ne uspijemo dogovoriti oko toga koju ćemo verziju povijesti imati, a kamoli da učimo ljude da vježbaju demokraciju."

Umjesto reprodukcije znanja, zagovara **znatiželju i kritičko mišljenje**: da čovjek, kad ga nešto "začeška", zna otići i iskopati podatak – nebitno je li to Aleksandrijska knjižnica, LLM ili Nacionalna i sveučilišna knjižnica – i saznati što točno kao građanin može učiniti da se nešto promijeni. To, kaže, traži cijelu jednu kulturu društva, a Hrvatska je izašla iz socijalizma "gdje je bilo zabranjeno misliti i propitivati", pa tu kulturu tek treba uzgojiti.

Organizirano lobiranje prema **saborskim odborima** smatra savršeno legitimnim i poželjnim: "Hrvatski sabor je pravo mjesto za te teme." Dovoljno inteligentan zastupnik, kaže, na takav input organizirao bi okrugli stol i pozvao medije. Kada voditelj pita može li i građanin pokrenuti okrugli stol u Saboru, gošća iskreno priznaje da ne zna – nikad to nije radila – ali upućuje na Poslovnik Hrvatskog sabora, koji je, uvjerena je, "do centimetra propisan i javno dostupan".

Realnost primanja građana ocjenjuje trezveno. Od ukupnog broja zastupnika, procjenjuje, možda će ih **sedamdesetak to rado napraviti, sedamdesetak neće jer čuvaju neku poziciju u stranci i boje se primati građane, a sedamdesetak im se jednostavno neće dati**. Uvijek je, kaže, u svakom sazivu bilo zastupnika kod kojih se moglo pokucati i ući, koji saslušaju sve ljude i o tome ne pričaju "jer su takvi ljudi" – ali i onih koji uvijek nađu razlog: nemaju drugu stolicu u uredu, nemaju tehničke mogućnosti ili su zauzeti stranačkim obvezama.

Isto vrijedi i na lokalnoj razini. Gradonačelnik, objašnjava, možda neće primiti osobno, ali primit će osoba zadužena za konkretan problem, jer je gradonačelnik dužan postupati u okviru Zakona o lokalnoj i područnoj samoupravi i statuta grada ili općine.

sections.subtitle_en: Who should teach citizens democracy – and who actually receives them
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest speaks about education, critical thinking, and the legacy of socialism
sections.content_en:
To the question of who should teach citizens how the system works, the guest is skeptical toward the institution of school. "Who should teach that – kindergarten, elementary school, high school? Why, we fail to agree on which version of history we will have, let alone teach people to practice democracy."

Instead of reproduction of knowledge, she advocates **curiosity and critical thinking**: that a person, when something "scratches" him, knows how to go and dig up data – regardless of whether it is the Library of Alexandria, an LLM, or the National and University Library – and find out what exactly as a citizen he can do to change something. That, she says, requires a whole culture of society, and Croatia emerged from socialism "where it was forbidden to think and question", so that culture has yet to be cultivated.

Organized lobbying toward **parliamentary committees** she considers perfectly legitimate and desirable: "Hrvatski sabor is the right place for these topics." A sufficiently intelligent representative, she says, on such input would organize a round table and invite the media. When the host asks whether a citizen can also launch a round table in the Sabor, the guest honestly admits that she does not know – she has never done it – but refers to the Standing Orders of the Hrvatski sabor, which, she is convinced, are "prescribed to the centimeter and publicly available".

She assesses the reality of receiving citizens soberly. Out of the total number of representatives, she estimates, maybe **about seventy will gladly do it, about seventy will not because they are guarding some position in the party and are afraid to receive citizens, and about seventy simply will not feel like it**. Always, she says, in every convocation there have been representatives whose doors could be knocked on and entered, who listen to all people and do not talk about it "because they are such people" – but also those who always find a reason: they do not have a second chair in the office, they do not have technical possibilities, or they are busy with party obligations.

The same applies at the local level. The mayor, she explains, might not receive personally, but the person in charge of the concrete problem will receive, because the mayor is obliged to act within the framework of the Local and Regional Self-Government Act and the statute of the city or municipality.

sections.subtitle: Šljunak, proračun i rok: pravo na pristup informacijama kao svakodnevni alat
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava obvezu javnih tijela da odgovore na predstavke građana
sections.content:
Uz pravo da ga se primi, građanin ima i mehanizam koji ne traži nikakav sastanak: **pravo da piše i dobije odgovor**. Sva tijela, ističe gošća, dužna su u zakonskom roku odgovoriti na svaku predstavku građana. "To je notorna stvar i to bi ljudi trebali znati i koristiti."

Primjer koji navodi krajnje je prizeman i zato uvjerljiv. Ako u godišnjem proračunu postoji stavka da se sve ceste pošljunčaju, a građanin utvrdi da njegova cesta ove godine nije prošla, ima puno pravo napisati upit: bilo je u proračunu, zašto nije učinjeno, kada će biti javni radovi. **I odgovor mora dobiti** – bio on "po planu je", "ostali smo bez para" ili "bit ćete sljedeći tjedan".

Logika je, kaže, ista bez obzira na razinu – lokalnu ili državnu: **"Mi porezni obveznici smo građani koji plaćamo za sve te javne usluge, mi moramo dobiti te javne usluge, a kad ih ne dobijemo moramo dobiti objašnjenje zašto ih nismo dobili."** Kakvo god objašnjenje bilo, ono se mora dati.

Pravo na pristup informacijama tako, zaključuje, nije egzotičan pravnički institut nego "potpuno obična stvar" primjenjiva na bilo koje javno tijelo koje se financira iz državnog proračuna.
sections.subtitle_en: Gravel, budget, and deadline: the right to access information as an everyday tool
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the obligation of public bodies to respond to citizens' petitions
sections.content_en:
Along with the right to be received, a citizen also has a mechanism that does not require any meeting: **the right to write and receive an answer**. All bodies, points out the guest, are obliged within the statutory deadline to respond to every citizen's petition. "That is a notorious thing and people should know and use that."

The example she cites is extremely down-to-earth and therefore convincing. If in the annual budget there is an item that all roads be graveled, and a citizen determines that his road did not pass this year, he has full right to write an inquiry: it was in the budget, why was it not done, when will public works take place. **And he must receive an answer** – whether it is "it is according to plan", "we ran out of money", or "you will be next week".

The logic is, she says, the same regardless of the level – local or national: **"We taxpayers are citizens who pay for all these public services, we must receive these public services, and when we do not receive them we must get an explanation why we did not receive them."** Whatever the explanation may be, it must be given.

The right to access information thus, she concludes, is not an exotic legal institute but a "completely ordinary thing" applicable to any public body financed from the state budget.

sections.subtitle: Milijun i 360 tisuća onih koji nisu izašli: matematika propuštene vlasti
sections.screenshot_description: Voditelj iznosi izračun prema kojem su neizašli birači mogli formirati vlast
sections.content:
Pred kraj ove cjeline razgovor se vraća na brojke – i one su brutalne. Na posljednjim parlamentarnim izborima, navodi se, **milijun i 360 tisuća ljudi nije izašlo na birališta**, dok je oko **700 tisuća glasova bilo dovoljno za osvajanje većine**.

Zaključak voditelja je neumoljiv: ljudi koji se nisu pojavili **mogli su četiri godine biti vlast**. Umjesto toga, kaže, "žele samo trolati na internetu" i po kafićima objašnjavati kako ništa ne valja, a ne čine ništa da to promijene. Njegov je poziv izravan: osnujte udrugu, osnujte stranku, potrudite se nešto naučiti, mijenjajte sustav iznutra ili izvana, lobirajte – **to je demokracija**.

Gošća se nadovezuje podsjećanjem da neke države kažnjavaju neizlazak: u Australiji je kazna 140 dolara, a u Belgiji, kaže, postoje kazne s uzlaznim stupnjevanjem. Ističe da razlog nije financiranje izbora, nego nešto zabrinjavajuće: **"Moraš kažnjavati ljude da bi ono što bi trebalo biti njihovo pravo – kao sloboda – ne izbjegavali."**

Suštinu vidi u nerazumijevanju vlastite pozicije u društvu. Kao što ne smijemo bacati smeće po cesti ili ubiti drugog čovjeka, tako smo dužni i **aktivno činiti stvari – izlaziti na izbore**. To nije samo pravo, nego i odgovornost. "Mi koji volimo prava, a ne volimo odgovornosti", ironizira, dodajući da je pretpostavka svake slobode upravo odgovornost.

Onima koji nisu zadovoljni vladajućima nudi jednostavan recept: organizirajte se, osnujte stranku, radite u njoj dvadeset godina, dođite do pozicije saborskog zastupnika, premijera i promijenite ono što vam se ne sviđa. **"To je cijela logika demokracije koja nije savršena, ali je najbolje što smo do sada smislili."** Alternative koje nabraja – tiranija, ropstvo, monarhija – teško da su bolje. Kada voditelj u šali spomene Vatikan kao model, gošća odbija ideju da o zemaljskim stvarima odlučuje jedan čovjek pozivajući se na Duha Svetoga.

Na voditeljevu opasku da smo "tu samo privremeno", gošća odgovara biblijskom prispodobom o talentima: **"Što si napravio s onim što si dobio – jesi li ih oplodio ili ćeš vratiti isti broj?"** Njezin zaključak: dužni smo vidjeti gdje smo najbolji i tu dati sve od sebe, a demokracija je za to idealan teren.
sections.subtitle_en: A million and 360 thousand of those who did not turn out: the mathematics of missed power
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host presents a calculation according to which non-turnout voters could have formed the government
sections.content_en:
Toward the end of this unit, the conversation returns to numbers – and they are brutal. In the last parliamentary elections, it is stated, **a million and 360 thousand people did not turn out to the polls**, while about **700 thousand votes were enough to win a majority**.

The host's conclusion is relentless: the people who did not show up **could have been the government for four years**. Instead, he says, they "only want to troll on the internet" and explain in cafes how nothing is good, while doing nothing to change it. His call is direct: establish an association, establish a party, make an effort to learn something, change the system from within or from outside, lobby – **that is democracy**.

The guest follows up with a reminder that some states penalize non-turnout: in Australia the fine is 140 dollars, and in Belgium, she says, there are fines with ascending grading. She points out that the reason is not financing the elections, but something worrying: **"You have to punish people so that what should be their right – like freedom – they would not avoid."**

She sees the essence in the misunderstanding of one's own position in society. Just as we must not throw garbage on the road or kill another human being, so we are also obliged to **actively do things – turn out for elections**. That is not only a right, but also a responsibility. "We who love rights, but do not love responsibilities", she ironizes, adding that the prerequisite of every freedom is precisely responsibility.

To those who are not satisfied with the ruling authorities she offers a simple recipe: organize yourselves, establish a party, work in it for twenty years, reach the position of member of parliament, prime minister, and change what you do not like. **"That is the whole logic of democracy, which is not perfect, but is the best we have come up with so far."** The alternatives she lists – tyranny, slavery, monarchy – are hardly better. When the host jokingly mentions the Vatican as a model, the guest rejects the idea that an earthly matter should be decided by one man invoking the Holy Spirit.

To the host's remark that we are "here only temporarily", the guest replies with the biblical parable of the talents: **"What did you do with what you received – did you make them fruitful or will you return the same number?"** Her conclusion: we are obliged to see where we are best and give our all there, and democracy is an ideal terrain for that.

sections.subtitle: „Kome je puno dano, od njega će se puno tražiti": poziv ljudima s publikom da siđu s tribine
sections.screenshot_description: Voditelj poziva vlasnike podcasta i ljude s velikom publikom da se politički angažiraju
sections.content:
Nakon biblijske digresije o talentima, u kojoj Marijana Šarolić Robić poručuje da je čovjek „dužan vidjeti gdje je najbolji i tu dati sve od sebe", voditelj razgovor prelama u konkretan apel. Parafrazirajući evanđeosku misao da će se od onoga kome je puno dano puno i tražiti, on se izravno obraća ljudima koji već imaju izgrađenu publiku.

„Postoje neki podcasti koji imaju pedeset tisuća followera", ističe voditelj, „pa ta osoba može sutra biti zastupnik i mijenjati stvari sa saborske govornice, a ne samo govoriti u mikrofon kako bi trebalo." Njegova poanta je da se retorika kondicionala mora zamijeniti prvim licem: **nema „trebalo bi", nego „ja ću, preuzimam na sebe i to ću izmijeniti"** — uz jasnu obvezu prema onima koji te podrže da će konkretna „rupa na cesti" doista biti zatrpana.

Marijana Šarolić Robić u tome prepoznaje pojam za koji hrvatski jezik, tvrdi, nema pravi ekvivalent:

- **responsibility** — odgovornost u smislu „kome ćemo poslati račun", pasivna kategorija koju imamo;
- **accountability** — aktivna odgovornost, preuzimanje posljedica vlastitih obećanja, koju, kaže, nemamo ni kao riječ ni kao naviku.

No, dodaje, to ne znači ništa loše samo po sebi: „To samo znači da imamo dijagnozu i sad znamo kako to promijeniti." Njezin zaključak je izravan poziv publici: što god vam se ne sviđa — mijenjajte, aktivirajte se, educirajte se i zagovarajte ono što mislite da treba biti drugačije. Sreća je, naglašava, što živimo u društvu u kojem se to čini bez mača i puške i bez trovanja protivnika, nego javnim zagovaranjem i skupljanjem dovoljnog broja ljudi koji te podržavaju.
sections.subtitle_en: "To whom much was given, of him much will be required": a call to people with an audience to step down from the stands
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host calls on podcast owners and people with a large audience to engage politically
sections.content_en:
After the biblical digression about the talents, in which Marijana Šarolić Robić conveys that a person is "obliged to see where he is best and give his all there", the host shifts the conversation into a concrete appeal. Paraphrasing the evangelical thought that from him to whom much was given much will be required, he speaks directly to people who already have a built audience.

"There are some podcasts that have fifty thousand followers", points out the host, "so that person can tomorrow be a representative and change things from the parliamentary rostrum, and not only speak into a microphone about how it should be." His point is that the rhetoric of the conditional must be replaced by the first person: **there is no "it should be", but "I will, I take it upon myself and I will change that"** — with a clear obligation toward those who support you that a concrete "pothole in the road" will indeed be filled in.

Marijana Šarolić Robić recognizes in this a concept for which the Croatian language, she claims, has no real equivalent:

- **responsibility** — responsibility in the sense of "to whom will we send the bill", a passive category that we have;
- **accountability** — active responsibility, taking on the consequences of one's own promises, which, she says, we do not have either as a word or as a habit.

However, she adds, that does not mean anything bad in itself: "That only means that we have a diagnosis and now we know how to change it." Her conclusion is a direct call to the audience: whatever you do not like — change it, get active, educate yourselves, and advocate for what you think should be different. The good fortune is, she emphasizes, that we live in a society in which this is done without sword and rifle and without poisoning opponents, but through public advocacy and gathering a sufficient number of people who support you.

sections.subtitle: „Nikad nismo živjeli bolje": tri generacije, osjećaj socijalne nepravde i znanje udaljeno jedan klik
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća uspoređuje život svoje bake, majke i sebe te tvrdi da prosječan građanin nikad nije imao više
sections.content:
Voditelj otvara tezu da živimo „u najboljem trenutku povijesti koji je itko ikad živio", a gošća je bez zadrške potvrđuje. Koliko god, kaže, otvaranje novina sugeriralo suprotno, to je „potpuna laž" — a mjeri to najosobnijim mjerilom koje ima: kako je živjela njezina baka, kako njezina majka i kako živi ona sama.

Govori isključivo iz hrvatske perspektive, naglašava, ne iz nizozemske ili neke druge, i zaključuje da **prosječan građanin nikad nije imao više nego što ima danas**. Istodobno priznaje da se osjećaj socijalne nepravde razlijeva na dva suprotna pola — na one koji žale za Jugoslavijom i one koji žale za velikom Hrvatskom. Poanta, tvrdi, nije u nostalgiji nego u odgovornosti: to blagostanje treba podizati dalje, a ne „reterirati", i to zbog sebe, zbog djece i zbog svih koji čine društvo.

Drugi argument tiče se znanja. Nikad, kaže Šarolić Robić, znanje nije bilo doslovno „one click away":

- svi su alati dostupni — treba samo sjesti, učiti, tražiti i povezivati;
- **umjetna inteligencija otključava resurse do kojih se ranije nije moglo doći**;
- ali sve to ima smisla samo uz kritičko promišljanje i namjeru da se stvari pomaknu nabolje, i to ne samo za sebe.

Voditelj dodaje da je tehnologija uvijek neutralna, s čime se gošća slaže: vrijednosni predznak dajemo mi. Odgovornost je, ponavlja, uvijek na pojedincu — na onome tko „stišće gumbiće", ali i na onome tko dopusti da se preko njega gumbići stišću. Svoju misao ilustrira banalnim, ali rječitim primjerom: nemojte vjerovati da je neko piće bez kalorija samo zato što tako piše u oglasu, jer deklaracija na proizvodu kaže drugo. „To pretpostavlja da staneš i pročitaš", kaže — dakle dodatni trud, umjesto naknadnog vapaja da su nas prevarili.
sections.subtitle_en: "We have never lived better": three generations, the feeling of social injustice, and knowledge one click away
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest compares the lives of her grandmother, her mother, and herself, claiming that the average citizen has never had more
sections.content_en:
The host opens the thesis that we live "at the best moment in history that anyone has ever lived", and the guest confirms it without hesitation. However much, she says, opening the newspapers suggests otherwise, that is "a complete lie" — and she measures it by the most personal standard she has: how her grandmother lived, how her mother lived, and how she lives herself.

She speaks exclusively from the Croatian perspective, she emphasizes, not from the Dutch or some other, and concludes that **the average citizen has never had more than he has today**. At the same time, she admits that the feeling of social injustice spills over into two opposite poles — to those who mourn for Yugoslavia and those who mourn for Greater Croatia. The point, she claims, is not in nostalgia but in responsibility: that prosperity should be raised further, not "backtracked", and that for oneself, for the children, and for all who make up society.

The second argument concerns knowledge. Never, says Šarolić Robić, has knowledge been literally "one click away":

- all tools are available — one only needs to sit down, learn, search, and connect;
- **artificial intelligence unlocks resources that could not be reached previously**;
- but all of that makes sense only with critical thinking and the intention to move things for the better, and that not only for oneself.

The host adds that technology is always neutral, with which the guest agrees: we give the value sign. Responsibility is, she repeats, always on the individual — on the one who "presses the buttons", but also on the one who allows buttons to be pressed through him. She illustrates her thought with a banal, but eloquent example: do not believe that a drink is zero calories just because it says so in the advertisement, because the declaration on the product says otherwise. "That assumes that you stop and read", she says — thus additional effort, instead of a subsequent cry that we were deceived.

sections.subtitle: „Nije važno tko će napraviti dobre stvari": zašto nam ipak još trebaju strukture
sections.screenshot_description: Voditelj citira poruku iz footera stranice nezavisne liste, gošća objašnjava potrebu za strukturom
sections.content:
Uz spomen platforme Nezavisni HR, voditelj u razgovor uvodi i lokalnu inicijativu Nezavisni VG te citira rečenicu koju je pronašao u podnožju njihove stranice: **nije važno tko će napraviti dobre stvari, važno je da se odrade**. Sam odmah dodaje ironičnu ogradu — kad bi svi tako razmišljali, ne bi nam trebale ni organizacije ni stranke, ali dok ne dođemo do te faze, one su nužne.

Marijana Šarolić Robić se slaže: dok se ne dosegne stanje u kojem su svi usmjereni na to da rade dobre stvari, „treba nam još uvijek strukture jer nažalost ne ide". To je, kaže, pitanje faze razvoja društva.

Razgovor se potom prelama na temu nasljeđa. Gošća povezuje simboliku (spominjući i hrvatski grb koji je bio i prije nas i bit će poslije nas) s idejom baštine: ako doista mislimo da nam je Hrvatska važna i da je to naslijeđe vrijedno prenijeti djeci, onda ga treba čuvati i živjeti, a ne uzimati zdravo za gotovo. Riječ je, kaže, o *heritageu* i *legacyju* — dijelu osobnog, građanskog i narodnog identiteta.

Najoštriju opomenu izriče o samoj demokraciji: **u trenutku kad je izgubiš iz fokusa, ona regresira**. Upravo to, tvrdi, vidimo u zrelim demokracijama koje odlaze u ekstreme — jer ljudi nisu izlazili na izbore i jer im nije bilo stalo. Ako se društvo mijenja u tom smjeru, dodaje, moramo barem biti svjesni da je to i naš izbor, ili preuzeti odgovornost i pobrinuti se da se dobre stvari naprave, nebitno tko ih je napravio.
sections.subtitle_en: "It does not matter who will do good things": why we still need structures after all
sections.screenshot_description_en: The host quotes a message from the footer of the independent list's website, the guest explains the need for structure
sections.content_en:
Along with mentioning the platform Nezavisni HR, the host introduces into the conversation the local initiative Nezavisni VG and quotes a sentence he found in the footer of their page: **it does not matter who will do good things, it is important that they are done**. He immediately adds an ironic caveat himself — if everyone thought like that, we would not need either organizations or parties, but until we reach that phase, they are necessary.

Marijana Šarolić Robić agrees: until a state is reached in which everyone is focused on doing good things, "we still need structure because unfortunately it doesn't work otherwise". That is, she says, a question of the development phase of society.

The conversation then shifts to the topic of heritage. The guest connects symbolism (also mentioning the Croatian coat of arms, which existed before us and will exist after us) with the idea of heritage: if we really think that Croatia is important to us and that this legacy is worth passing on to children, then it should be preserved and lived, not taken for granted. It is, she says, about *heritage* and *legacy* — part of personal, civic, and national identity.

She issues the sharpest warning about democracy itself: **the moment you lose it from focus, it regresses**. That is precisely, she claims, what we see in mature democracies that go to extremes — because people did not turn out for elections and because they did not care. If society is changing in that direction, she adds, we must at least be aware that that is also our choice, or take responsibility and make sure that good things are done, regardless of who did them.

sections.subtitle: Četrnaest ljudi za listu — i onaj nevidljivi posao koji sve ruši
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava zašto se nezavisne inicijative najčešće raspadnu na izgradnji strukture
sections.content:
Voditelj se prisjeća prethodne epizode i razgovora s Ivanom Orulovićem u kojoj je zaključeno da za izlazak na izbore u jednoj izbornoj jedinici doslovno treba **četrnaest ljudi voljnih stati na listu** — bez ikakve stranke.

Marijana Šarolić Robić ne spori matematiku, ali upozorava da se podcjenjuje sve ono što dolazi poslije. Proces od inicijative do stranke, kaže, mučan je posao. Četrnaest nezavisnih može proizvesti i samo konfuziju ako iza njih ne stoji infrastruktura koja će rezultirati stvarnim glasovima i kasnijim odlukama.

Kao dokaz navodi domaće primjere — inicijative poput Možemo!, Mosta i drugih koje su uspjele okupiti nezavisne, a onda su, tvrdi, zapele na „sitnom kokošarenju": tko je kome dao donaciju, tko gura koju cestu, koju zemlju treba staviti ili izbaciti iz građevinske zone. Podsjeća i na SDP koji se, kaže, urušio unatoč tome što je desetljećima bio stranka i partija.

Nasuprot tome, kao primjer organizacijske izvrsnosti navodi HDZ: „Oni su i dalje savršena organizacija", kaže, jer imaju jasno postavljene ciljeve i hijerarhiju operacija — pa zato imaju i *delivery*. Politička stranka na kraju, tvrdi, mora funkcionirati kao korporacija.

Paralelu povlači sa start-up svijetom:

- **slaganje procesa i operacija je nevidljiv posao bez kojeg ništa ne može postojati**;
- u politici je pandan onome što poduzetnici zovu *bootstrapping* — dizanje na vlastite noge do *product market fita* i prihoda, kad ti više nijedan investitor ne treba jer ti je tržište najbolji kupac;
- ideju treba pokrenuti, pa je onda ili pivotirati ili od nje odustati — ali nikako ne odustati unaprijed.
sections.subtitle_en: Fourteen people for a list — and that invisible work that tears everything down
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains why independent initiatives most often fall apart over building structure
sections.content_en:
The host recalls the previous episode and the conversation with Ivan Orulović in which it was concluded that to run in an election in one constituency literally takes **fourteen people willing to stand on a list** — without any party.

Marijana Šarolić Robić does not dispute the math, but warns that everything that comes after is underestimated. The process from an initiative to a party, she says, is grueling work. Fourteen independents can produce merely confusion if behind them there is no infrastructure that will result in real votes and subsequent decisions.

As proof, she cites domestic examples — initiatives like Možemo!, Most, and others that managed to gather independents, and then, she claims, got stuck on "petty squabbling": who gave a donation to whom, who is pushing which road, which land should be placed in or removed from the construction zone. She also recalls the SDP, which, she says, collapsed despite being a party for decades.

In contrast, as an example of organizational excellence she cites the HDZ: "They are still a perfect organization", she says, because they have clearly set goals and a hierarchy of operations — which is why they also have *delivery*. A political party in the end, she claims, must function like a corporation.

She draws a parallel with the start-up world:

- **arranging processes and operations is invisible work without which nothing can exist**;
- in politics, the counterpart is what entrepreneurs call *bootstrapping* — standing up on one's own feet until *product market fit* and revenue, when you no longer need any investor because the market is your best customer;
- an idea should be launched, and then either pivoted or abandoned — but by no means abandoned in advance.

sections.subtitle: Rokovi za EU Inc: rujan na Europskom vijeću, primjena od siječnja
sections.screenshot_description: Gošća objašnjava vremenski plan usvajanja EU Inc regulative
sections.content:
Vrativši se na glavnu temu epizode, Marijana Šarolić Robić poziva sve koji o tome mogu govoriti da EU Inc-u daju vidljivost. Vremenski plan koji navodi je konkretan:

- **u devetom mjesecu** tekst bi na Europskom vijeću trebao proći „u formi u kojoj treba";
- nakon toga slijedi izglasavanje i implementacija;
- **cilj je da od siječnja iduće godine EU Inc vrijedi na razini cijele Europske unije**.

Na pitanje voditelja hoće li se Hrvatsku „stisnuti" da to implementira, gošća odgovara da je pitanje pogrešno postavljeno: nije riječ o hrvatskom, nego o europskom propisu, a **rokove određuje Europski parlament, ne pojedina država**. Tu, kaže, počinje igra lobiranja: veliki će kupovati vrijeme. Hrvatska bi, tvrdi, to mogla „jedan-jedan", jer joj je infrastruktura spremna, dok Njemačkoj treba dodatnih godinu dana da uspostavi tehničke pretpostavke za takav registar — koji, dodaje, nemaju ni za svoja obična trgovačka društva.

Uloga udruge, objašnjava, jest pritisak: kroz CroStartup, Allied for Startups i European Startup Network vrši se pritisak na političare da rok bude najkraći mogući, bilo da je to šest mjeseci ili godina dana, i to na europskoj razini — jer nema smisla da Hrvatska EU Inc ima, a Njemačka ne. Vjeruje da će Europska komisija gurati brzo, jer joj je stalo da to bude njezina velika pobjeda u aktualnom mandatu.

Šire posljedice su, kaže, veće od samog osnivanja firme. EU Inc je ključan dio *Scaleup* politike jer otvara vrata drugim mjerama, poput **Scaleup fonda i obveze da se dio mirovinskog novca ulaže u europske start-upove**, umjesto da taj kapital odlazi isključivo u američke tehnološke kompanije. Krajnji cilj koji formulira glasi: doći do toga da Europa uopće ima jednoroge koji u Ameriku moraju ići tek zbog IPO-a i exita — jer od te faze, priznaje, „jako, jako smo daleko".
sections.subtitle_en: Deadlines for EU Inc: September at the European Council, application from January
sections.screenshot_description_en: The guest explains the timeline for the adoption of the EU Inc regulation
sections.content_en:
Returning to the main topic of the episode, Marijana Šarolić Robić calls on everyone who can talk about it to give visibility to EU Inc. The timeline she provides is concrete:

- **in the ninth month** the text should pass at the European Council "in the form in which it should";
- after that comes voting and implementation;
- **the goal is for EU Inc to be valid at the level of the entire European Union from January of next year**.

To the host's question whether Croatia will be "squeezed" into implementing it, the guest answers that the question is wrongly phrased: it is not about a Croatian, but a European regulation, and **deadlines are determined by the European Parliament, not an individual country**. Here, she says, the lobbying game begins: the big ones will buy time. Croatia, she claims, could do this "one-on-one", because its infrastructure is ready, while Germany needs an additional year to establish the technical prerequisites for such a registry — which, she adds, they do not even have for their ordinary commercial companies.

The role of the association, she explains, is pressure: through CroStartup, Allied for Startups, and the European Startup Network, pressure is exerted on politicians so that the deadline is the shortest possible, whether that is six months or a year, and that at the European level — because it makes no sense for Croatia to have EU Inc, and Germany not to. She believes that the European Commission will push fast, because it cares that this be its great victory in the current mandate.

The broader consequences are, she says, greater than the mere establishment of a company. EU Inc is a key part of the *Scaleup* policy because it opens the door to other measures, such as the **Scaleup Fund and the obligation to invest part of pension money into European start-ups**, instead of that capital going exclusively to American technology companies. The ultimate goal she formulates is: to reach a point where Europe has unicorns at all that have to go to America only for an IPO and exit — because from that phase, she admits, "we are very, very far away".
